sources.news_title: Anthropic Files S-1 for Nasdaq Listing Amid AI Safety Concerns
sources.text:
Anthropic has filed an S-1 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to list shares on the Nasdaq Composite Index under the ticker symbol "ANT." The filing marks the company's move toward an initial public offering, potentially as early as November, shifting its capital structure from private funding to public equity.
The offering serves as a valuation benchmark for the artificial intelligence sector, impacting not only the developer of the Claude platform but also the broader infrastructure of chipmakers and data center providers. While the influx of capital into AI has driven stock market indices to record highs, analysts at Lightshed note a stark divide in potential outcomes: the company could either become one of the world's most valuable entities or face bankruptcy.
This volatility is driven by a critical need for capital to maintain competitiveness against rivals like OpenAI. According to Lightshed, the speed of these public debuts leaves investors with limited time to evaluate the actual underlying assets and revenue models they are purchasing.
The push for public funding continues despite documented internal and external warnings regarding AI safety. In September, CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in development following a former researcher's estimate that there is a 10% probability the technology could lead to human extinction within ten years. Despite these warnings and reports of AI agents behaving unpredictably, Anthropic is proceeding with its market debut to secure the financial resources necessary for continued growth.

sources.news_title: Anthropic’s IPO Filing Includes Alarming Clauses About AI’s Potential Risks
sources.text:
Anthropic’s own IPO pitch to prospective investors has laid bare the company’s deep fears about where artificial intelligence could ultimately lead humanity.
The AI company is on course to pursue what could become Wall Street’s largest-ever initial public offering after filing to go public on Monday. Its valuation is reportedly expected to reach as much as $2 trillion.
Yet Anthropic’s IPO prospectus devotes an unusually large amount of space to philosophical and moral dilemmas—subjects rarely explored in such depth by companies seeking a stock-market listing.
The artificial intelligence company, led by the fiercely safety-focused Dario Amodei, has filled its investor presentation with stark warnings about AI’s potentially devastating consequences.
Amodei and his six co-founders wrote: ‘Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.’
Anthropic opens its prospectus with a sweeping assessment for potential investors: ‘We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history.’
But the optimism is quickly tempered by a warning: ‘If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.’
The 335-page filing, introduced with colorful graphics featuring cells and circular scientific imagery, then turns to the wide-ranging dangers associated with advanced AI.
The artificial intelligence company, led by the intensely safety-focused Dario Amodei, has filled its investor pitch with anxious warnings about AI’s potentially devastating power
People protest artificial intelligence and data centers ahead of a New York City Council Committee hearing on the risks and regulation of artificial intelligence
It states: ‘To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good.
‘Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.’
The language offers a pointed reference to Amodei’s sudden departure from OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company led by Sam Altman, where he worked until 2020.
Amodei left after trust in the company’s management broke down and disagreements intensified over AI safety and governance.
A year later, in 2021, he founded rival company Anthropic with his sister, Daniela.
The prospectus goes on to outline the threats facing the company and the wider world, including misuse, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption.
It warns: ‘Authoritarian governments may use AI to create high-tech surveillance states, deepen repression, and make themselves much more difficult to dislodge.
‘AI can be misused by those who wish to do harm, for example to conduct cyberattacks or to design biological weapons.’
Amodei said Anthropic already ‘regularly’ shuts down efforts by malicious actors to abuse its AI chatbots. That includes an incident earlier this year in which the Houthi terrorist group used Claude to help build ballistic missiles.
READ MORE: Report: Michigan Democrats Turn on Obama After Abdul El-Sayed Rally
The Anthropic chief then issued a chilling warning about what could happen if AI systems began operating independently, without human control.
‘[This] could be a global security threat of the first order.’
The Anthropic CEO also referenced how he’s aware the AI boom will likely mean entire workforces are wiped out, causing mass economic disruption ‘similar to what has happened with previous technologies… but greater in magnitude.’
Artificial intelligence has been compared to the Industrial Revolution in the way it is fundamentally changing the way we work, make money, and operate as a society.
Amodei said the company is committed to ‘running studies’ to help governments figure out how best to deal with potential economic downfalls triggered by AI.
The CEO’s biggest concern is also written out in the prospectus – the fact that his technology ‘poses catastrophic or existential risk to humanity.’
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and owner of X, formerly known as Twitter, Anthropic Co-Founder and Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown, and Atreides Management Managing Partner and Chief Investment Officer Gavin Baker during National Design Studio’s launch event for America.gov in September
People protest artificial intelligence and data centers ahead of a New York City Council Committee
This ultimate risk factor, Amodei hopes, can be mitigated if the tech is ‘developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures.’
But apart from the serious notes of doom and gloom, Anthrophic used their opening IPO letter to gush about the ways in which their super technology is helping humanity.
‘In California, Claude is helping to shorten the lines at the DMV, and to better serve people on Medicaid. In the United Kingdom, it is helping job seekers find their way through government services.’
Amodei lead on its successes with breakthroughs that AI can make in biology and medicine, namely to cure diseases that have ‘plagued humanity for millennia.’
He hinted that more innovation is on the horizon – including making a tool for gene editing.
‘We have started to directly make biological discoveries with Claude: among them is the discovery of a molecular machine that might have the potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool, perhaps for gene editing.’
Rather idyllically, Amodei also painted a picture where his AI can ‘bend the arc of geopolitical history in the direction of freedom.’
And at the pinnacle, Anthrophic wants to ‘ensure that free societies,’ like the United States, ‘lead in the world’s most powerful technology.’
Amodei finished the prospectus by saying: ‘We hope you will see it as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.
‘We have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.’

sources.news_title: Anthropic Files for Potentially Largest IPO in History, Seeking Valuation of Up to $2 Trillion
sources.text:
The artificial intelligence company behind Claude has submitted public offering documents that could lead to a record-breaking $100 billion stock sale, revealing surging revenue, substantial losses and an unusual ownership structure designed to preserve founder control.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, filed documents Monday, Oct. 26, for an initial public offering that could raise as much as $100 billion and value the company at up to $2 trillion, potentially making it the largest IPO in stock market history.
The San Francisco-based company submitted its registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission, disclosing rapid revenue growth alongside substantial financial losses and extraordinary spending commitments needed to compete in the expanding artificial intelligence industry.
According to Anthropic’s official SEC filing, the company intends to list its Class A common shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. The offering could take place as early as November, although Anthropic has not disclosed a final date, share price or number of shares to be sold.
The potential $100 billion offering would exceed the $29.4 billion raised by Saudi Aramco in its 2019 IPO, currently recognized as the largest initial public offering in history. However, the proposed fundraising amount and valuation remain estimates rather than confirmed terms.
Anthropic’s public filing follows a confidential registration submitted in June, when the company was valued at approximately $965 billion following a $65 billion private funding round. The contemplated public valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion would represent another substantial increase for a company founded only five years ago.
The Associated Press reported Monday that Anthropic’s offering could test investor willingness to finance the increasingly expensive race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, particularly as technology companies face growing questions about profitability and infrastructure spending.
The registration documents provide one of the most detailed public examinations of Anthropic’s finances since its founding in 2021 by former OpenAI executives, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Anthropic reported approximately $16.3 billion in revenue during the first six months of 2026, compared with roughly $1.1 billion during the corresponding period in 2025. The increase reflects accelerating demand for Claude, particularly among businesses incorporating artificial intelligence into software development, research and other operations.
Despite that growth, the company recorded a net loss of approximately $80.7 billion during the first half of 2026. Much of that amount resulted from accounting adjustments associated with convertible debt and other financial instruments rather than ordinary operating expenses.
The figures nevertheless underscore the considerable financial demands associated with training and deploying increasingly sophisticated AI models.
The company reported an operating loss of $693 million for the first six months of 2026, while adjusted operating income reached approximately $1.62 billion, compared with a $1.85 billion adjusted operating loss a year earlier. Reuters reported that Anthropic’s revenue for the second quarter increased 1,368% from the same period last year.
Anthropic has also committed substantial resources to cloud computing and specialized infrastructure necessary to train and operate its AI systems. Those obligations create financial risks as the company competes with OpenAI, Google and other developers of advanced artificial intelligence.
The proceeds from the IPO would support infrastructure expansion, operating expenses, research, employee recruitment and potentially acquisitions. Anthropic said it has not entered into agreements for any material acquisitions.
The company’s customer base has expanded rapidly. According to the prospectus, more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30% of businesses in the Global 2000 generated at least $100,000 in revenue for Anthropic during the 12 months ending Sept. 30.
Its enterprise-focused services have become an important source of growth, particularly as companies integrate Claude into coding, document analysis, customer support and other business applications.
Anthropic’s proposed public listing also reveals an unusual corporate governance structure intended to preserve its founders’ influence while maintaining oversight of AI safety.
Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, and Daniela Amodei, its president, will share control of a special class of stock with five other co-founders. Those shares will collectively carry 50.1% of the company’s shareholder voting power, allowing the founders to retain majority control after the public offering.
A separate Long-Term Benefit Trust will possess authority to appoint and remove directors occupying a majority of the board’s authorized seats. The trust is intended to ensure that the company balances financial interests with its stated mission of developing advanced AI responsibly.
Anthropic is organized as a Delaware public benefit corporation, a structure requiring directors to consider the interests of stockholders, people affected by its activities and the company’s designated public benefit purpose.
The arrangement could limit the influence of ordinary public shareholders over major corporate decisions, an issue disclosed among the risks associated with investing in the company.
The prospectus also includes extensive warnings concerning the potential misuse of artificial intelligence.
Anthropic identifies risks involving cyberattacks, the development of chemical weapons, government surveillance and increasingly autonomous AI systems whose capabilities could exceed existing safety controls.
In its filing, the company warns that advanced models may produce outputs that “could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative,” including conduct resembling blackmail.
Anthropic also acknowledges that using artificial intelligence to accelerate its own research could create additional challenges for safety testing and oversight.
“Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures,” the company stated in its prospectus.
Dario Amodei has publicly advocated slowing certain aspects of AI development to allow safety precautions to keep pace with technological advances. His position has distinguished Anthropic from competitors emphasizing rapid deployment and commercial expansion.
The company has also been involved in a dispute with the Trump administration over the use of its technology for military applications.
In February, President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth criticized Anthropic after the company resisted permitting unrestricted military uses of its AI technology. The Pentagon subsequently designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, prompting legal challenges.
Anthropic sued the Defense Department in March, alleging that the designation constituted unlawful retaliation. Separate federal court rulings have produced conflicting outcomes, and both sides are pursuing appeals.
The controversy highlights the competing demands Anthropic faces as it seeks government contracts, commercial customers and public-market investment while maintaining restrictions on certain applications of its technology.
The IPO also comes during heightened scrutiny of the broader AI industry.
Investors have increasingly questioned whether companies can generate sufficient profits to justify spending hundreds of billions of dollars on chips, data centers, electricity and computing infrastructure.
Several major technology companies have disclosed expanding capital expenditure plans, raising concerns about borrowing costs and the potential for excess infrastructure capacity if demand falls short of expectations.
Anthropic’s financial disclosures illustrate that tension. Its revenue growth demonstrates substantial commercial demand, while its losses and financing obligations reveal the costs of remaining competitive in advanced AI development.
The public offering could establish an important valuation benchmark for other privately held AI developers, particularly OpenAI, which has also explored a potential stock market listing.
A successful offering would give Anthropic access to substantial new capital and provide existing shareholders with opportunities to sell portions of their holdings. It could also make the company’s seven founders among the wealthiest technology entrepreneurs.
Nevertheless, the proposed valuation and fundraising target remain uncertain. The final offering will depend on SEC review, market conditions, investor demand and decisions by Anthropic and its underwriters.
If Anthropic raises the reported $100 billion, it would surpass the $86 billion generated by SpaceX’s June 2026 public offering, establishing a new IPO fundraising record.
With its registration documents now public, Anthropic is moving closer to a stock market debut that could significantly reshape the competitive and financial landscape of artificial intelligence.

Plus, one big opportunity for climate change.
Anthropic is worried about its ability to power data centers.
While much of the company’s more-than-330-page filing for its planned initial public offering focuses on the mundane (executive compensation) and the extraordinary (“existential risks” are mentioned three times), considerable space is devoted to the problems of power.
The word “energy” appears 14 times in the section of the document laying out risks to Anthropic’s business, while “climate” or “climate change” is mentioned four times.
The overarching concern the company has is that it might not get enough power for data centers running its large language models. “Delays in securing energy, water, and other critical services for these facilities could further slow the pace at which newly commissioned compute becomes available for use,” is one representative sample from its risk factors section. The document later notes that “our business may face increased scrutiny related to these activities … including from the investment community and the local communities in which we operate,” in a later section on environmental, social, and governance standards.
Anthropic is also concerned with the pace of the energy infrastructure build-out more generally, noting “the construction of the generation and transmission infrastructure on which we depend is itself capital-intensive and exposed to labor shortages, supply chain disruptions, permitting delays, changes in interest rates, tariffs, other cost overruns, and financing constraints.” These concerns will be familiar to anyone following the debate in Washington, D.C., over permitting reform, which is also centered on making transmission easier and cheaper to build.
Later in the document, Anthropic writes that electricity policy is both highly varied across the country — “Grid-tied electrical supply, for instance, is subject to the jurisdiction of federal and state energy regulators, regional grid operators, and public utility commissions” — and also evolving, noting specifically that “environmental standards applicable to power generation continue to evolve, including as a result of changing governmental priorities and shifting public and political views regarding climate change and the appropriate treatment of various power generation sources.”
The risk of these policies is that they could result in “failure to secure access to adequate electrical power,” which could then “adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.”
Anthropic also acknowledges energy can be quite expensive, writing that costs are “largely outside of our control” and can “rise sharply during periods of peak demand or constrained supply, and such increases in energy costs could adversely affect our results of operations.”
Anthropic is the charter member of an industry group, along with Nvidia and Google, to promote and enable demand flexibility, which would reduce peak demand — and thus bring down electricity prices and alleviate the need for additional new infrastructure — by having data centers draw down their power usage when demand was at its highest. The company notes that it has also signed on to “voluntary commitments to offset the impact of our data center energy consumption on local communities and electricity ratepayers.” Already, the document says, “these commitments have increased, and we expect will continue to increase, our operating costs.”
And while the document has little to say about climate change per se and even less about sustainability and renewables, it does note that “the physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time, as higher average temperatures can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend.”
Climate change also acts as an amplifier for potential disasters that could affect the company. “The impact of climate change may increase these risks,” the company says of “war, terrorist attacks, and other acts of political violence, or any significant natural disaster, such as an earthquake, fire, hurricane, tornado, flood, or significant power outage.”
Specifically, Anthropic calls out climate-related risk specific to the Bay Area, where it is headquartered. Or, as it bloodlessly describes it, “a region known for seismic activity and increasingly for the threat of fires.”
Otherwise, climate change and sustainability policy is largely seen as a regulatory and cost burden. For example, “regulations relating to [environmental, social, and governance] matters, including environmental sustainability and climate change, are under consideration, being adopted, or being rolled back or revised, which may impact our necessary disclosures and increase compliance costs,” and “sustainability initiatives, goals, or commitments could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement.”
It notes a variety of California, European Union, and United Kingdom climate disclosure laws “will require the dedication of significant time and resources” while also observing that “across the United States ... enacted or proposed ‘anti-ESG’ policies or legislation or have issued related legal opinions,” which could “expose any sustainability, employment, governance, or other corporate practices we adopt to the risk of litigation, antitrust investigations or challenges by federal or state authorities, and result in injunctions, penalties, and reputational harm.”
The document is far less detailed about what Anthropic and its products could do to alleviate or prevent climate change and its effects. This is not surprising for a regulatory filing concerned with disclosing corporate information and outlining risks to investors — but the filing is also supposed to explain the business opportunities it sees as well. In that regard, climate is relegated to a laundry list of potential scientific projects Anthropic’s products could be helpful with. “Claude is also being applied to pressing global problems in scientific research, drug discovery, education, and climate analysis,” it writes.
If its S-1 is any indication, there will be a lot of work to do.

sources.news_title: Anthropic's IPO filing shows $16.3bn of revenue and no plan to sell ads
sources.text:
Anthropic has never sold an advertisement, and the document it filed on Monday gives no sign that it intends to. The company behind Claude submitted a registration statement on Form S-1 to the Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, seeking to list Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker "ANT". The filing reports revenue of $16.286 billion for the six months to June 30, 2026, against $1.163 billion a year earlier, earned from metered usage of its models and from subscriptions. There is no ad tier, no sponsored answer and no audience product in it.
That absence is the obvious headline for a marketing audience. It is also slightly misleading. Read through its exhibits, the prospectus describes a company sitting unusually close to the centre of the advertising economy, only from the other side of the ledger. Its two largest compute suppliers, Google and Amazon, run two of the biggest advertising businesses in the world. Both hold stakes in it, both resell its models through their cloud marketplaces, and in the first half of 2026 Amazon booked more income from its Anthropic investment in a single quarter than it earned from advertising. Anthropic does not sell ads; its rise has been reported, in part, inside the earnings of companies that do.
Six of the publications PPC Land readers follow carried something bearing on Anthropic on Monday. PPC Land published four articles on the filing in the late afternoon, UTC. Adweek and MediaPost each ran their own reading of it. PPC News Feed and AdExchanger covered the tools and the measurement problems that sit downstream of Claude, and Search Engine Roundtable's daily recap pointed to a fresh lawsuit. Taken together, they describe a business that has grown roughly fifteen-fold in a year without a single advertiser, and a set of commitments that will take a decade or more to pay off.
What the filing shows
PPC Land reported at 16:31 UTC on October 26 that Anthropic files for Nasdaq IPO with $16.3bn in first-half revenue. The registration, file number 333-299633, leaves the price range and the number of shares blank. Its revenue history is short and steep: $41 million in 2023, the first year of commercial sales, $386 million in 2024 and $4.585 billion in 2025. The first quarter of 2026 brought $4.731 billion and the second $11.555 billion.
Adweek's Trishla Ostwal, publishing at 12:02 Eastern time the same day, reported that Anthropic goes for the public markets as revenue jumps nearly 15-fold. Second-quarter revenue of $11.56 billion compared with $787 million a year earlier. The filing puts the growth in plain terms: revenue "grew 1,368% year-over-year for the three months ended June 30, 2026" while compute and infrastructure expenses "grew 300%". Those costs fell to 48% of revenue from 251% in the first quarter of 2025. Operating income in the second quarter was $974 million, the only profitable quarter among the results Anthropic disclosed.
The half-year picture is less tidy. PPC Land put the operating loss for the first six months of 2026 at $693 million, down from $2.135 billion a year earlier; set against Adweek's second-quarter profit, that implies a first-quarter operating loss of roughly $1.67 billion. The net loss for the half was $80.748 billion, of which $72.388 billion was a non-cash change in the fair value of convertible notes, derivatives and simple agreements for future equity. The 2025 net loss was $41.965 billion. Anthropic also presents a non-GAAP adjusted operating margin of 10%, which excludes stock-based compensation; that compensation rose to $2.2 billion in the half, from $286 million, for a headcount of about 5,300.
The company is not short of cash. It held $131.651 billion at June 30, 2026, made up of $112.4 billion in cash and $19.3 billion in short-term investments, and had raised $141.1 billion in total by the same date. "Our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance," the prospectus warns, in the sentence every growth company includes and few have had as much reason to.
Some of the most watched numbers are missing. The filing gives third-quarter revenue only as a multiple, 86 times the fourth quarter of 2024, which PPC Land converts to about $16.9 billion. Run-rate revenue as of October 31, 2026 is left blank, though the definition is printed: trailing 28-day consumption fees multiplied by 13, plus monthly subscription fees multiplied by 12. MediaPost's Laurie Sullivan reported on June 1, when Anthropic first filed a draft IPO registration, that the annualised run rate had reached $47 billion, up from $9 billion at the end of 2025, with more than 80% of revenue coming from enterprise clients.
The customer base explains where that money comes from. As of September 30, 2026, more than 11,900 customers generated over $100,000 each in trailing revenue, up from more than 950 a year earlier, Adweek reported. More than 1,900 paid over $1 million and about 250 over $10 million. Roughly 40 million customers each spend less than $100,000. Net revenue retention was about 900%, a figure PPC Land notes excludes Claude Pro and Max subscribers. Adweek found that the top five customers accounted for about 25% of revenue in the nine months to September 30 and that no single customer exceeded 10%; PPC Land flagged another reading of the filing in which two customers made up about one-fifth of revenue, and said the accounts may not be fully contradictory.
What investors will pay remains a matter of press reports rather than disclosure. The Wall Street Journal reported, as relayed by Adweek, that Anthropic could raise $100 billion or more at a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, with a listing targeted for the week of November 16. The fee table in the filing uses a placeholder maximum offering price of $1 billion, on which Anthropic paid a registration fee of $87,000. Twenty-two underwriters are named, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.
The road here has been quick. Adweek reported on June 1 that Anthropic files for IPO as AI race hits public markets, days after a $65 billion Series H round at a $965 billion post-money valuation. A week later, on June 8, Adweek reported that OpenAI confidentially filed for an IPO, saying it "may be a while" before any offering. Monday's Adweek piece notes that OpenAI is not expected to list until 2027, which would make Anthropic the first standalone American frontier AI lab to trade publicly. Little more than a year ago, in September 2025, PPC Land reported that Anthropic completed a $13 billion Series F at a $183 billion valuation. The Series E, in March 2025, had valued it at $61.5 billion.
A business with no ad tier
MediaPost's editor in chief, Joe Mandese, searched the 557-page document for an advertising business and reported on October 26 that the Anthropic IPO omits any plans for an ad model. Advertising is not listed as a potential business model. The word appears, as does "media", but mostly in reference to Anthropic's own marketing rather than to an ad-supported product. Mandese ran keyword counts: "agent" was too frequent to tally, and among the words he selected, "human" ranked highest, followed by "marketing", "agentic", "autonomous" and "subscription". The filing never uses the word "extinction".
There is a small irony in the method. To summarise the business model, Mandese used Google's Gemini, which described two revenue lines: consumption-based metering, in which enterprise customers and developers pay for Claude usage measured in tokens, and fixed monthly subscriptions such as Claude Pro and Claude Max. The prospectus says nothing about serving ads, monetising user data through ad networks or offering an ad-supported tier.
That is consistent with what Anthropic has said publicly. On February 4, 2026, the company pledged that Claude would remain free of advertising on every subscription tier, and PPC Land reported the next day that Anthropic dropped millions on a Super Bowl ad savaging OpenAI's ChatGPT ad pivot. The four commercials, two of them set to air during Super Bowl 60 on February 8, carried the line "Ads are coming to AI. But not to Claude." OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman responded on X that evening, and on February 5, in a live interview, called Anthropic's Super Bowl ads dishonest. OpenAI went the other way: PPC Land's timeline in Monday's coverage records ChatGPT ads launching in the United States on February 9 and passing a $1 billion annualised run rate by August 31.
The pledge does not mean Anthropic stays away from paid media. Laurie Sullivan noted in MediaPost on March 27 that Anthropic ran a connected TV ad about Claude that month. What the filing shows is that its commercial spending has gone somewhere else. Sales, marketing and partnerships expense reached $3.168 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $120 million a year earlier. PPC Land attributes most of that increase to a $2.7 billion rise in fees paid to channel partners rather than to advertising. Anthropic records sales through the cloud marketplaces gross and books the providers' cut as an expense, so much of the line where a media budget would normally sit consists of fees to the partners that resell Claude.
The consumer numbers help explain why advertising was never the obvious route. Emarketer, cited by MediaPost in June, forecast that 5.4% of US internet users would use Claude in 2026, against 36.6% for ChatGPT and 27.4% for Gemini. An ad business needs reach. Anthropic built a revenue line larger than many ad businesses without it, by selling to companies that pay by the token. PPC Land estimates annualised revenue of roughly $46 billion, none of it from advertising.
The landlords sell ads
The second PPC Land piece, published at 16:49 UTC, followed the money the other way. It reported that Amazon, Google and Microsoft hold $269bn of Anthropic compute contracts. The commitments are at least $114.5 billion to Google Cloud, running from April 2026 to July 2033 and payable "regardless of actual usage"; at least $110.0 billion to Amazon, from May 2026 to April 2036; and at least $44.9 billion to Microsoft Azure, from November 2026 to May 2033. The $269.4 billion sum of those minimums excludes about $161.2 billion of TPU-based equipment leases from Broadcom, up to $120.5 billion from SpaceXAI, a SpaceX subsidiary, and the cloud fees already mentioned.
How large the full bill is depends on who is counting. The filing describes total purchase commitments as "more than $" and leaves the number blank. Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre summed four non-cancellable lines to $430.6 billion; Cape Fear Advisors added SpaceXAI, Nscale and Lambda to reach $637.0 billion; ZeroHedge, including AMD and future TPU estimates, put it at about $780 billion to $810 billion; and Reuters, cited by Investing.com, used a narrower accounting measure of about $245 billion plus about $21 billion in short-term obligations. Adweek reported that Anthropic expects to spend another $125 billion to $150 billion on Google TPU capacity from 2028 to 2031, and that the Journal puts total compute obligations above $475 billion. Investing.com warned that the figures cover different agreements and should not simply be added.
"We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners," the prospectus says. The partners are also, in nearly every case, investors, sales channels and competitors. Claude is "accessible on all three major cloud platforms," and sales through the Amazon, Google and Microsoft marketplaces made up about 48% of first-half revenue, by coincidence the same proportion as the compute cost ratio Adweek reported, or roughly $7.8 billion on PPC Land's arithmetic, up from 32% in 2024 and 47% in 2025. Marketplace sales also accounted for 58% of net receivables at June 30. A large share of Anthropic's customers, in other words, pay the hyperscaler, which pays Anthropic, which pays the hyperscaler again for compute.
For the advertising market, the more striking numbers sit in the suppliers' own accounts. Amazon invested $8 billion in Anthropic convertible notes between the third quarter of 2023 and the fourth quarter of 2025, and booked a $16.8 billion non-cash gain in the first quarter of 2026 when part of them converted. In the second quarter it reported $53.4 billion of non-operating other income, "primarily from the company's investments in Anthropic." On PPC Land's calculation, that was more than two and a half times Amazon's $19.8 billion of advertising revenue in the same quarter. As far back as October 2025, PPC Land reported that Amazon advertising hit $17.7B as AWS accelerated with an Anthropic AI cluster, when Project Rainier came online with nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips and Amazon recorded a $9.5 billion pretax gain on its stake.
Alphabet's position is murkier because it does not tie its gains to specific holdings. Its second-quarter net income included $77.1 billion of net unrealised equity gains, in a quarter when Google Search ads generated $63.3 billion; first-quarter other income was $37.7 billion. Analyst estimates of Alphabet's Anthropic stake range from 10% to 15%. The same quarter brought capital expenditure of $44.9 billion and negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion. PPC Land's argument is that a growing share of the headline earnings at both companies reflects Anthropic's valuation rather than advertising, and that these non-cash gains can reverse once the market puts a price on the stock.
Microsoft agreed in November 2025 to invest up to $5 billion, and Nvidia up to $10 billion in the same month; Nvidia GPUs sit behind the SpaceXAI, Nscale and Lambda capacity, about $206.4 billion combined. SpaceXAI alone runs to about $3.1 billion a month. Meta has no disclosed equity or compute link at all, but in April it opened Ads AI Connectors that let Claude create and edit campaigns through its ads server, as PPC Land reported when Meta opened its ad system to Claude and ChatGPT on April 29, 2026. Apple's only documented connection is as a participant in Project Glasswing.
The concentration has drawn regulators before. In July, France's competition authority found that OpenAI, Google and Anthropic together held more than 84% of the global AI agent sector in May 2026, PPC Land reported when it covered how France flags lock-in risk as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic hold 84% of AI agents. The S-1 adds a less visible kind of concentration, in which the lab's suppliers and its rivals are the same few firms.
Paper instead of cash
The fourth PPC Land article, published at 17:57 UTC, went through the exhibits. It reported that Anthropic IPO exhibits show 9% interest on Broadcom's $42bn chip notes. The registration, accession number 0001628280-26-067168, carries 33 exhibits and 44 graphics files, and many commercial terms are redacted under Item 601(b)(10)(iv) of Regulation S-K.
The Broadcom arrangement is the most unusual. Under a note purchase agreement effective March 31, 2026, Broadcom committed $42 billion, and the notes cover the quarterly fees under a chip lease in place of rent. Interest runs at 9.00%, or 13.00% during a "Breach Period", and is capitalised each quarter rather than paid. "In no event shall any amount drawn on a Note be paid in cash," the agreement states. On PPC Land's arithmetic, $1 billion drawn at 9% grows to about $1.56 billion after five years, and to about $1.90 billion at 13%. The notes convert at 90% of the market price, or 85% in a breach period, into non-voting N-Class stock, and if Anthropic is sold Broadcom can choose conversion or cash at 150% of the amount outstanding. The first $24 billion matures at five years, and there is no prepayment without Broadcom's consent. A registration rights agreement dated June 8, 2026 was signed for Anthropic by its chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, and for Broadcom by Mark Brazeal, its chief legal and corporate affairs officer.
The chips themselves come from Google. A master equipment lease for TPU8i hardware, also effective March 31, names Broadcom as lessor and AI Infrastructure OpCo II, LLC as lessee, with Anthropic as guarantor. The hardware supplier is Google LLC, code-named "Enso", which sells to Broadcom. Rent is paid in 20 quarterly instalments over five years, orders cannot be cancelled and there is no right of set-off. "Lessee shall make its claim solely against Enso," the lease says. The pods must be delivered to data centres in the contiguous United States, and Google and its affiliates cannot act as approved operators. In effect, Anthropic leases Google-made chips through Broadcom, can settle the fees with notes that compound, and cannot have Google operate the hardware.
Google's own financing is partly tied to Anthropic's sales. A $30 billion note purchase agreement, the $40 billion total less Google's Series G investment, has two draw periods: the first tied to delivered TPU capacity, the second to a "Company Revenue Attainment Percentage" measured against a redacted revenue target, which Google can defer. Both end on December 31, 2030. An IPO Acceleration Option allows Google to buy up to $10 billion of N-Class stock at the IPO price, and its stake is capped at 14.99% of fully diluted capitalisation, with any excess pushed into ten-year Roll-Over Notes paying 0.00%. A registration rights agreement dated May 4, 2026 states that Anthropic does not consider Google an affiliate. Adweek added that Google put $10 billion and Amazon $5 billion into the Series H round.
Amazon's facility, dated April 20, 2026, has a ceiling of $20 billion that stood at zero on signing and rises by $5 billion for each unit of delivered capacity, the unit itself redacted. "No interest shall accrue on this Convertible Promissory Note," the form states. Amazon's ownership is capped at 12% of partially diluted capitalisation, and the facility expires 30 months after listing. In section 5(k), Anthropic "does not warrant that it will achieve any results projected in the Business Plan."
The remaining exhibits fill in the rest of the balance sheet. A credit agreement dated September 4, 2026 names Morgan Stanley Senior Funding as agent on a reported $15 billion facility, with a margin of 1.000% until two of S&P, Moody's and Fitch award investment-grade ratings. Anthropic subleases about 230,208 square feet at 500 Howard Street from Salesforce until August 30, 2028, and has leased about 483,844 square feet at 300 Howard Street from January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2038. Salesforce is thus its landlord, a channel partner and, through Salesforce Ventures, an investor. The pre-IPO charter puts the Series A price at $2.5656 a share and the Series H-1 price at $589.0095, both before a 10-for-1 split, a gap PPC Land calculates at about 230 times.
Who holds the vote
Public shareholders will own a great deal of the economics and very little of the control. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holds a single Class T share, with no economic rights, which elects the directors who form a majority of the board. Its trustees are Ben Bernanke, Richard Fontaine and Neil "Buddy" Shah, with Bryn Mawr Trust Company of Delaware as administrative trustee. Anthropic Founders, LLC holds one Class F share, also without economic rights, carrying 50.1% of the total vote on most matters. Its seven members are Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah; a footnote reportedly states that Benjamin Mann, another co-founder, is not a member. "Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the LTBT and the Founder LLC," the prospectus acknowledges.
The structure has a sunset. If fewer than three continuing founders remain for 90 consecutive days, a 450-day transition begins, after which the Class F and Class E shares are redeemed for nothing. Class E stock, intended for non-founder employees, can be redeemed without payment if a holder joins what the company, in its sole discretion, deems a "Direct Competitor". The stockholders' agreement names Chris Liddell as the "Specified Class T Director" and gives the trust a five-day notice right over transfers of control of advanced AI models. The credit agreement's change-of-control trigger sits at 50.0%, a tenth of a point below the founders' vote.
The stated purpose is "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." An Anthropic Public Benefit Fund received 846,840,960 Class N shares, described as 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026. Two charity proxy agreements, with the Dechomai Asset Trust and the Daffy Charitable Fund, were signed by Dario Amodei for the company and as proxyholder, who may act "in his or her sole and absolute discretion (including for any reason or no reason)." The donation agreements themselves are not filed.
Investors, meanwhile, keep their options open. The investors' rights agreement, which names Spark Capital, Salesforce Ventures, Menlo, Lightspeed, ICONIQ and GIC's Greenview Investment, lets them back competing companies, subject to exceptions. Employees who join a rival can lose their Class E stock; investors who fund one face no such penalty.
What marketers are buying
If advertising is absent from the business model, marketers are hardly absent from the user base, even though the filing never names them. PPC Land reported at 16:43 UTC that Claude Opus 5.5 cuts cost per task 40%, the Anthropic IPO filing says. "Claude Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs per task by approximately 40% compared to Claude Opus 5," the filing states, with no methodology. The logic Anthropic draws from it is volume: "Lower costs per task drive greater usage, which in turn drives broader diffusion of Claude." Cheaper tasks, in this account, mean more tasks, and more tokens billed.
The prospectus describes three products. The Claude Platform is "our comprehensive agentic development environment." Claude Code, "our coding agent," entered research preview in February 2025, and NASA engineers used it to plan navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover. Claude Cowork, "our knowledge work agent," followed as a research preview in January 2026, and in September 2026 Anthropic began merging Cowork with Claude.ai. All three are framed as "Virtual Collaborators", agents that carry "the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them." The filing says "non-technical teams" are adopting Claude Code and Cowork; it does not say which.
Spending per seat is modest. Citing the S-1, WebProNews reported that non-coding Claude Enterprise users averaged under $75 a month, while the top 5% of Claude Code adopters spent roughly 20 times that. Fortune 500 customers in the $100,000-plus tier spent less than 0.1% of their total expenses with Anthropic. Customers pay by tokens or through fixed-price subscriptions, but the filing gives no plan prices for Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise, no customer return-on-investment data and no revenue breakdown by business function.
The marketing integrations are documented elsewhere, mostly in PPC Land's own archive. The Trade Desk's chief executive Jeff Green confirmed in March that a closed beta lets advertisers build campaigns with Claude, PPC Land reported when The Trade Desk tested Claude for campaign creation on March 14. Digiday's Krystal Scanlon reported on May 18 that the company was showing agencies its Koa Agents, which can connect to Claude through an interoperability layer, in a piece inside The Trade Desk's Claude-powered campaign agent; the agents were designed to wait for marketer sign-off before acting. Semrush released a Claude connector on August 26 drawing on 28.8 billion keywords, PPC Land reported when Semrush gained a native Claude connector, although its listed capabilities were read-only. The same day, Salesforce and Anthropic announced an expanded partnership, and PPC Land reported that Salesforce puts 37 prebuilt sales skills inside Claude for pilot customers.
Anthropic's own marketers are a test case. In July, PPC Land reported that Claude Cowork cut Anthropic's weekly report build from two days to two hours, in an account by Ian Chan and Annabel Custer of its marketing operations team. A weekly metrics report that had taken one to two days now ran on a Sunday-evening schedule in up to two hours.
On Monday the ad platforms kept opening their doors. PPC News Feed reported at 12:00 UTC that the Microsoft Ads MCP adds asset performance and change history, a change spotted by Hana Kobzová. Two new tools join Microsoft Advertising's MCP server. GetAssets returns performance for text, image and video assets, linked to accounts, campaigns or ad groups, with a default 30-day window. GetChangeHistory provides a sortable log of account changes covering up to 180 days. Claude is named among the interfaces that can connect, with ChatGPT, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot, and the setup now accepts personal as well as work or school Microsoft accounts. The detail matters in light of the S-1: Microsoft invested in Anthropic and is owed at least $44.9 billion for Azure capacity, and its ad platform is now handing Claude the data to judge which headlines work.
Not every consequence of that shift is visible to the people paying for media. Writing in AdExchanger at 04:35 UTC on October 26, Margarita Savytska of Sojourn Solutions argued that B2B buying decisions are moving where ad tech can't see. When an AI assistant researches and recommends a vendor, no impression, click or cookie is recorded. "Impressions are measured. Decisions aren't," she wrote. Her example is a campaign that reaches 1,000 buyers already in the market and claims 50 conversions, when an incrementality test suggests 45 of them would have happened anyway. She does not name Anthropic, but the S-1 describes precisely the kind of tool she means: an assistant embedded in enterprise work, sold by the token, that carries no ads and therefore leaves no ad-tech trace.
The risks in the small print
Adweek counted 94 pages of risk factors, which it described as nearly a quarter of the filing; MediaPost's page count of 557 suggests a smaller share, so the two tallies do not quite reconcile. PPC Land counted 18 summary risks. Several read like nothing else in a prospectus. "Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways," the summary states. Models, "including our own, have exhibited, and may in the future exhibit, unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown," Adweek quoted. Anthropic also warned that "no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity" to cover a catastrophic AI-related incident.
Other risks are more familiar to anyone who has put a frontier model into a marketing workflow. The filing defines hallucination as output that is factually incorrect "with apparent confidence." In an NP Digital test of six platforms with 600 prompts, reported on February 2, Claude was fully correct 55.1% of the time against 59.7% for ChatGPT, but had the lowest error rate, at 6.2%, PPC Land reported when nearly half of marketers said they encounter AI errors weekly. Anthropic says it "may in the future change" usage and rate limits, that forced retirement of older models could cause customers to leave, and that it may delay releases for safety reasons. Its example is Claude Mythos, released to a restricted group through Project Glasswing on April 7, 2026; Mozilla later fixed 271 Firefox security bugs found with Mythos Preview. The Daily Brief, cited by PPC Land, reported that export restrictions in June 2026 forced Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 temporarily.
The filing also discloses four incidents in which models gained unauthorised access during misconfigured evaluations, and records a revenue problem of Anthropic's own making. About 7% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 came from customers later found to have violated its usage policy or commercial terms, Adweek reported, without the filing specifying the violations. Enforcement stepped up in August and September, which Anthropic said "may reduce our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods." It is an unusual disclosure: a company telling prospective shareholders that turning away some customers will cost it growth. "A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of customers," it adds.
Courts, Washington and copyright
The most expensive risk to have materialised so far has been legal. The prospectus records the $1.5 billion Bartz settlement, about $3,000 for each of roughly 500,000 books, booked as a 2025 operating expense. It lists as pending the second suit from music publishers, filed on January 28, 2026, which PPC Land reported when music publishers sued Anthropic for $3 billion over pirated songs; the filing counts 20,517 compositions, and the claim rests on statutory damages. Reddit's scraping claims went back to California state court in March. Another claim surfaced the day before the filing: Search Engine Roundtable's daily recap for October 26 pointed to a New York Times report, dated October 25, that the owners of Elvis Presley's music have sued Anthropic for copyright infringement.
Publishers, by contrast, have mostly left Anthropic alone. Adweek's Mark Stenberg observed on August 26 that Anthropic has never signed a licensing deal, yet never been sued by a premium digital publisher, unlike OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and Perplexity, all of which have signed some form of content deal. What Anthropic has done is publish the rules for its bots. In February, PPC Land reported that Anthropic clarified what its three web crawlers do: ClaudeBot for training, Claude-User for fetching pages when a user asks, and Claude-SearchBot for search relevance.
The dispute with Washington is the strangest item in the risk section. On February 27, 2026, President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic's technology, which the filing says came "in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance." The Secretary of War moved to designate Anthropic a "supply-chain risk to national security." On March 26, Judge Rita F. Lin granted a preliminary injunction in the Northern District of California, as PPC Land reported when a judge blocked the Pentagon from blacklisting Anthropic, describing the government's actions as "classic illegal First Amendment retaliation." Adweek reported that Anthropic won most of its case at district level in August, that an appeals court ruled 2-1 against it on part of the designation in September, and that it has asked the full appeals court to reconsider. Government contracts are about 1% of revenue, and Anthropic says it "cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies."
Commercially, the fight may have helped. Digiday's Krystal Scanlon reported on March 9 that Anthropic's Pentagon refusal was paying off in downloads, brand trust and enterprise deals. Claude's iOS app reached first place on Apple's US free chart over the weekend of February 28 to March 1, having sat at 131st on January 30. Pulsar sentiment scores put Anthropic at 63.9 against 49.3 for OpenAI after OpenAI's Pentagon deal, and Ramp data showed 56% of organisations using a generative AI vendor using Anthropic, up from 29% a year earlier. A brand built on refusing advertising, and then on refusing a government, has turned out to be worth something in the enterprise market. Whether that holds once the company answers to public shareholders is the question the governance structure is meant to settle.
November 16
If the Journal's timetable holds, Anthropic will list in the week of November 16, about three weeks from the filing. Before then the blanks must be filled: the price range, the share count, the aggregate compute commitment and the amounts due within twelve months. The third-quarter revenue figure, now visible only as a multiple of a quarter nearly two years old, will have to appear in dollars.
For the advertising industry, the listing will settle a narrower question as well. Amazon has recorded tens of billions of dollars of gains on its Anthropic holding this year, and Alphabet's unrealised equity gains, which it does not attribute to specific holdings, reached $77.1 billion in a single quarter, at a time when both companies' advertising businesses were growing. Once Anthropic trades, those holdings will be marked to a public price every day, and part of what two of the largest sellers of digital advertising report as profit will move with the shares of a company that sells no ads at all. Anthropic kept advertising out of Claude. It has not kept Claude out of advertising's results.

sources.news_title: Anthropic preps for initial public stock offering in major step for AI company
sources.text:
Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, filed papers Monday to prepare for a potential initial public offering (IPO), taking a major step toward a listing on public markets.
The long-anticipated move comes months after Anthropic said it had “confidentially submitted a draft registration statement on Form S-1” with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Monday’s filing touts AI as “one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.”
At the same time, “To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” Anthropic’s filing says, noting that AI “can be misused by those who wish to do harm” and “may also behave autonomously in ways we (and our users) do not intend — as illustrated by recent high-profile cybersecurity incidents. Losing control of sufficiently powerful AI systems could be a global security threat of the first order.”
“We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level,” the filing says.
Public concern over the possible risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from AI-related security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company.
In July, Anthropic said a review of more than 140,000 testing runs of its AI models had unearthed three separate self-directed cyberattacks against other organizations.
Rival companies, including OpenAI, have also revealed AI-related security incidents in recent months.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last month announced a precautionary slowdown of AI development to ensure sufficient risk prevention. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also said last month he would dial back the pace of his company’s AI development.
Anthropic earned $16.3 billion in revenue over the first six months of this year, growing nearly 14-fold from $1.2 billion in revenue in the same period a year earlier, the company’s filing said.
Still, the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion over the first six months of this year, indicating the scale of its spending over that period.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

sources.news_title: Anthropic files for IPO in historic Nasdaq debut, revealing $16.3B in revenue and staggering $80.7B loss - Tech Startups
sources.text:
Anthropic files for IPO in historic Nasdaq debut, revealing $16.3B in revenue and staggering $80.7B loss
Anthropic, the five-year-old AI startup behind Claude, has officially filed for an initial public offering, setting the stage for one of the largest stock market debuts in history. The company plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT,” according to its S-1 registration statement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Monday.
The IPO could value Anthropic at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, according to market estimates reported by The Wall Street Journal. The company could raise $100 billion or more through the offering, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record $85.7 billion IPO earlier this year. Anthropic has yet to disclose its proposed share price or the number of shares it plans to sell.
The filing offers a remarkable look inside one of the fastest-growing companies in the artificial intelligence industry. Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first six months of 2026, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier. But that growth came with an eye-catching $80.7 billion net loss, most of which stemmed from noncash accounting charges tied to the rising value of its convertible financing instruments.
Beneath that headline figure, Anthropic’s operating performance tells a different story. Its operating loss narrowed to $693 million from $2.14 billion a year earlier, even as demand for Claude and its AI coding tools surged among corporate customers.
The IPO arrives at a difficult moment for the broader AI industry. Wall Street is questioning whether enormous investments in data centers, computing infrastructure, and advanced AI models will generate sustainable returns. For Anthropic, the offering could become a defining test of investor confidence in generative AI economics.
Anthropic’s explosive growth comes with a staggering price tag
Founded in 2021 by Dario Amodei and a group of former OpenAI researchers, Anthropic has grown from a relatively small AI research startup into one of the industry’s most valuable private companies.
Its Claude models have gained traction among businesses, developers, and large enterprises seeking alternatives to OpenAI and Google’s AI offerings. Claude Code, the company’s AI coding assistant, has become a major contributor to that growth.
Anthropic’s IPO prospectus reveals that more than 11,900 customers were generating at least $100,000 in annualized revenue as of September 30, underscoring its growing presence in the enterprise market.
The financial details are striking. Of Anthropic’s $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026, approximately $72.4 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and related financial instruments. These accounting adjustments largely reflect the company’s rising valuation rather than cash spent on daily operations.
Still, running a frontier AI company remains extraordinarily expensive. Anthropic has made more than $600 billion in computing infrastructure commitments, according to Reuters, highlighting the enormous financial demands of developing and operating advanced AI systems.
The company faces fierce competition from OpenAI and Google, and depends on major technology partners for computing capacity and distribution.
A historic IPO with unusual shareholder control
Anthropic’s public offering follows SpaceX’s record-setting Nasdaq debut earlier this year, which raised $85.7 billion. The timing puts another closely watched technology company in front of investors already questioning the sustainability of AI spending.
The filing reveals an unusual corporate structure that could attract scrutiny from prospective shareholders.
Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting rights through a special entity called Founder LLC.
A separate Long-Term Benefit Trust will generally have authority to appoint a majority of the company’s board. The arrangement reflects Anthropic’s public benefit corporation structure and its stated commitment to responsible AI development, but it limits the influence ordinary shareholders can exercise over corporate decisions.
The prospectus identifies risks ranging from competition and mounting infrastructure expenses to AI safety concerns, regulatory disputes, and reliance on major cloud providers.
Amazon and Alphabet remain important investors and strategic partners. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the underwriting.
For Wall Street, the question goes beyond how much Anthropic is worth. Investors must decide whether one of the fastest-growing technology businesses can eventually turn extraordinary demand for AI into lasting profits.
Anthropic’s IPO may provide the clearest answer yet.

AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion
October 26, 2026
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic on Monday filed paperwork to make its stock market debut in what analysts say could be one of the biggest in history.
The initial public offering (IPO) could happen as early as November, reports say, with analysts putting the company at a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
What did the Anthropic founders say about the IPO?
The seven co-founders of the company, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, outlined their vision for the future of AI in a letter to potential investors.
"We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," they said.
The AI startup behind Claude also addressed the societal risks of AI as they have done before, writing that the company's leadership might have to take unusual decisions to slow down the pace of development, even if that meant falling behind competitors.
The filing toward an IPO represents a major milestone for a company that was founded just five years ago.
Money raised at the IPO could provide the company with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.
What do we know about Anthropic's IPO?
Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."
But the company is yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell and what price, leaving that space blank in its paperwork filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.
Anthropic filed confidentially with the SEC in June and that gave the agency time to go over the company's financial credentials before they were made available to the public and potential investors.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters.
Anthropic debut follows SpaceX IPO
The San Francisco-based company was founded by members who defected from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2021.
OpenAI, Anthropic's main rival, is also set to debut on the stock market next year.
Both IPOs are taking place amid growing concern about AI and the race to develop AI infrastructure, including data centers that consume vast amounts of energy.
The document filed by Anthropic shows that the company has seen massive revenue growth but is yet to turn a profit, much like its AI rivals.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, the company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30.
And as for money raised at the IPO, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX that ultimately raised $86 billion in what was the biggest IPO on record to date.

sources.news_title: Anthropic's IPO filing shows off soaring revenues as the company warns of AI's 'risks to humanity'
sources.text:
Anthropic warned AI could bring "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" if it is not "developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures."
US firm Anthropic gave the world a window into its remarkable finances on Monday after it submitted its S-1 paperwork ahead of a planned initial public offering.
The artificial intelligence company revealed soaring revenues and high costs as it warned of the risks posed by AI.
The listing will be a key yardstick for investor appetite in an increasingly controversial industry that has quickly woven itself into the fabric of daily life.
Anthropic's net losses hit $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, the filing showed, while revenue jumped to around $16.3 billion over the period.
An IPO could bring in as much as $100 billion for the company behind Claude, with it potentially valued at upwards of $1.5 trillion, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in May.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the company said in the S-1 form. "If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."
But Anthropic also warned of the dangers posed by its technology, saying AI could bring "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" if it is not "developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures."
"The political environment and our engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action," it added.
Gary Marcus, an emeritus professor at New York University and a staunch critic of the AI industry, accused Anthropic of attempting to "skirt the truth" with the filing by leaving out certain figures.

sources.text:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in the United States on Monday, moving closer to a stock market debut that could rank among the largest in history.
The San Francisco-based company plans to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT, according to its announcement. Anthropic has not yet determined the number of shares it will offer or the price range for the offering.
The company filed a registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The filing is not yet effective, and the shares cannot be sold until the registration becomes effective. The proposed listing comes as investors weigh the rapid growth of the AI industry against the substantial costs of developing and operating increasingly powerful models.
Revenue surges as losses mount
Anthropic reported revenue of $16.29 billion for the first six months of 2026, alongside a net loss of approximately $80 billion, according to its prospectus, according to The Guardian.
The company’s revenue has grown sharply over the past three years. It generated $41 million in 2023, $386 million in 2024 and $4.59 billion in 2025.
READ: Anthropic’s new AI agent Claude Duet can work while users are away (October 22, 2026)
The figures underline the rapid expansion of demand for Claude and Anthropic’s AI services, particularly among business customers. They also illustrate the financial pressures facing companies investing heavily in AI development and infrastructure.
Anthropic disclosed that it had raised $141.1 billion as of the end of June 2026. The Guardian reported that investors had valued the company at more than $1.5 trillion, while Reuters reported that some current and prospective investors were considering a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. Reuters also reported that Anthropic could seek to raise as much as $100 billion through the IPO. The company has not confirmed the final offering size or pricing.
Enterprise demand drives growth
Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister, Daniela Amodei, Anthropic develops AI models and products used for writing, software development, research and other business applications.
Its flagship product, Claude, competes with ChatGPT from OpenAI and other generative AI platforms. Anthropic has also expanded its coding tools and enterprise-focused services as companies adopt AI to automate tasks and support software development.
According to the prospectus figures cited by The Guardian, Anthropic had more than 14,000 enterprise customers as of Sept. 30. Of those, 11,900 generated at least $100,000 in revenue for the company, more than 1,900 generated at least $1 million, and about 250 generated at least $10 million.
However, the company also disclosed that a substantial portion of its revenue came from a limited number of customers. Its five largest customers accounted for about one-quarter of revenue, although no single customer represented more than 10%. Such concentration creates a potential financial risk if major customers reduce their spending or switch to competing AI services.
AI safety and business risks
Anthropic’s IPO filing also details risks associated with the technology it develops, including potential misuse of advanced AI systems, cybersecurity threats, loss of control and economic disruption.
The company has warned that its most capable models could provide assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop dangerous weapons. It also acknowledged that its technical safeguards are incomplete and could be bypassed or fail to operate as intended.
The Guardian reported that Anthropic disclosed an incident in September 2025 in which it assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group had manipulated its Claude Code tool in an attempted cyberattack targeting about 30 organizations worldwide.
READ: Anthropic posts $80.7 billion loss in first half of 2026 as AI infrastructure costs surge (October 21, 2026)
The disclosure places AI safety among the issues investors may consider when assessing the company’s long-term prospects, alongside revenue growth, competition and the cost of computing infrastructure.
Anthropic has also faced a dispute with the Trump administration over the use of its AI products in military operations. The company was designated a supply chain risk, a decision that restricts military agencies from contracting with it. Anthropic has challenged the designation.
A major test for the AI market
Anthropic’s proposed listing comes amid a broader race among AI companies to attract capital and expand their computing capacity.
Reuters reported that the IPO could test investor appetite for large AI businesses as companies spend heavily on models, data centers and specialized chips. The offering could also provide public-market investors with greater access to a sector that has largely depended on private funding.
OpenAI, Anthropic’s principal competitor, has also taken steps toward a potential public listing. However, Reuters reported that OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that the company would not go public in 2026.
For Anthropic, the IPO will provide an opportunity to raise capital from public investors while exposing its financial performance, business risks and governance to greater scrutiny. The final valuation, offering size and timing of the market debut remain subject to the IPO process and regulatory requirements.

Anthropic’s artificial intelligence (AI) lab lost almost $81 billion in first half of 2026.
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is set to make its long-awaited Wall Street debut as soon as November.
The artificial intelligence (AI) giant filed its Form S-1 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Oct. 26, setting the stage for its initial public offering—also known as an IPO.
It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT,” according to the prospectus.
Anthropic offered a deep dive into its first six months of financial results. It posted $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.16 billion in the same period a year ago—or 1,300 percent year-over-year growth—driven by heavy spending from leading AI hyperscalers.
The prospectus is absent an IPO valuation, but the company had previously targeted up to $2 trillion. Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in a funding round this past spring.
“We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth,” the San Francisco-based firm said in the document.
Because many firms rely on its technology, Anthropic reported that its client base is far more diverse than that of other companies in the industry.
“No single customer represented more than 10% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026,” Anthropic said in the filing.
The top five of its customers represented approximately 25 percent of its revenues.
The company acknowledged its net losses, noting that it might not “generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” It reported a net loss of almost $81 billion in the first half of the year, from $42 billion in all of 2025.
Growth prospects could “slow or stall” if demand for its applications, models, or platforms is slower than expected or declines, the company said. If so, its financial conditions and earnings results “could be adversely affected.”
