sources.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press By — Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/anthropic-files-for-potentially-the-biggest-ipo-ever-as-ceo-warns-of-ais-existential-risk-to-humanity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of AI's existential risk to humanity Nation Oct 26, 2026 12:40 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs. READ MORE: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars. The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, though its losses after taking out certain items were a fraction of that. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion. Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla. As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by one of Elon Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year. In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT." Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals. Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals. But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble. The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI's plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse in the coming months. Investors have become increasingly jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO. Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world. Reflecting AI's dangers, the document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic has also appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn't put financial interests ahead of public safety. READ MORE: AI discovered a software vulnerability that could impact 70% of websites worldwide. The rush is on to patch it Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of "risk factors," a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading. Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of "malicious actors" using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and, given the numerous hacking incidents from rogue AI agents recently, the possibility Anthropic's AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Calls for an AI slowdown The IPO comes as reports emerge about AI's ability to solve problems beyond human capacity for good, but also to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks while humans lose control. In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months. He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones. "I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei wrote. Clashes with the U.S. government Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the "good guys," focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs and with few guardrails. Some of this sentiment stems from the company's dispute with the U.S. government, which broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk. Anthropic sued the Pentagon over the supply chain risk designation in March for what it called an "unlawful campaign of retaliation" over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified an unusually public dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance. ChatGPT maker OpenAI made its own deal to work with the Pentagon hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk. A California judge ruled in Anthropic's favor in the first case and a Washington D.C. judge sided with the government in the second. Both sides are appealing the decisions. Digging Past the Headline Loss
Anthropic generated an impressive $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026. That figure sits alongside an $80.7 billion net loss. A cursory glance might suggest an unsustainable cash burn rate, but a balance sheet analysis tells a vastly different story.
Most of that $80.7 billion deficit is an accounting artifact: a non-cash charge driven by mark-to-market adjustments to derivative liabilities. One of the most revealing metrics buried within the filing is not the equity valuation but the scale of the vendor commitments. Amazon and Alphabet occupy a unique, vertically integrated position within the generative artificial intelligence ecosystem. Strategic investments in this space function as enclosed ecosystems, where institutional capital injections recycle back into the investors' cloud divisions via binding compute contracts.
The critical fundamental question is how these top-line guarantees flow through to cloud operating margins and free cash flow. While the revenue is secured, servicing an excess of $220 billion in compute demand requires aggressive capital expenditure cycles.
With both Amazon and Alphabet scheduled to report earnings this week, management commentary regarding capital expenditures and anticipated infrastructure amortization schedules will serve as immediate catalysts. Investors might watch these reports closely for signs of cloud margin expansion, which would validate the profitability of recycling venture investments back into enclosed compute contracts.

This capital outlay flows through a dual-track architecture pipeline. A large portion of the compute load relies on merchant silicon, reinforcing NVIDIA's NASDAQ: NVDA data-center dominance. sources.news_title: Anthropic S-1 shows $16.3B revenue and huge compute bills
sources.text:
Anthropic, PBC filed a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, October 26, 2026, and applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. Revenue for the first six months of 2026 reached $16.3 billion, a jump of about 1,300% from the $1.16 billion booked in the same stretch of 2025.
Neither the number of shares nor the price range has been filled in. Pitches to investors could begin as soon as the week of Nov. 9, according to reports, and the company is aiming for a haul that equals or tops the $85.7 billion SpaceX collected in its Nasdaq debut. Back in June, Anthropic said its confidential draft submission gave it “the option to go public after the SEC completes its review.”
Anthropic has confidentially submitted a draft S-1 registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Pending completion of SEC review, this gives us the option to pursue an initial public offering. Read more: https://t.co/onGZAhRLvD
— Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) June 1, 2026
Both the company and selling stockholders will offer Class A shares, though Anthropic will receive nothing from the stockholders’ portion. Underwriting duties fall to 22 banks, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley in the lead roles.
Governance runs through a public benefit corporation structure in which a Long-Term Benefit Trust picks most directors by way of a special class of shares. Co-founders hold voting control through a single Class F share, issued to a limited liability company they formed, that commands 50.1% of all votes. Nasdaq rules classify the company as a controlled company as a result.
The half-year net loss totals $80.7 billion, yet most of that figure involves no cash. Roughly $72.4 billion traces to the revaluation of convertible notes and similar instruments as the company’s worth climbed, and the cash-flow statement adds $8.72 billion in noncash charges on other financial instruments.
Operating figures are far smaller. Compute and infrastructure costs climbed to $8.95 billion from $2.33 billion, and the operating loss was $693 million, down from $2.14 billion a year earlier. Spending on personnel totaled $3.15 billion, and sales, marketing and partnerships added $3.17 billion.
Adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation, noncash charitable contributions and the Bartz settlement, was $1.62 billion, though standard accounting rules do not count it as profit. Cash from operations was positive at $3.93 billion, a result the company attributes partly to when customers paid and when vendors were paid. Liquidity at June 30 totaled $112.4 billion in cash and equivalents plus $19.3 billion in short-term investments.
Consumption-based fees made up 80% of first-half revenue, and a large share of it is not tied to multiyear customer contracts. Data center and cloud contracts run the other direction, since payments can continue for years on capacity that sits idle. One equipment lease alone requires roughly $125.2 billion in rent across five years, excluding interest.
Cross-defaults are a stated risk, since failing to meet particular obligations could trigger defaults in other contracts and threaten access to critical resources. In the past, the company has requested more capacity from cloud providers than they were willing to supply, and nothing in its contracts promises delivery by the date it wants.
By Sept. 30, more than 1,900 customers had each produced at least $1 million in revenue over the trailing 12 months, and about 250 of them reached $10 million or more. Customers topping $100,000 over the same period numbered more than 11,900.
Claude is meant to take on tasks with no fixed endpoint that last for weeks and, down the line, to run as millions of simultaneous copies, a destination the filing calls a “country of geniuses in a data center.” Recent agent work such as the Claude Duet preview points the same direction.
Legal footing for such agents is unsettled, according to the filing, which says it is unclear at what point an agent’s conduct could obligate the organization deploying it, and whether liability caps in contracts would hold if challenged. Resulting liabilities and security breakdowns might exceed what insurance would cover, it adds.
Regulators have also come calling: the Federal Trade Commission sent a civil investigative demand in October asking about consumer protection, data protection, privacy, product safety and security. Litigation over the Department of War’s supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic appears too, with a court ruling that went in the company’s favor before the D.C. Circuit denied its petition for review on Sept. 25 in a 2-1 decision. A petition for rehearing en banc has been filed with the full court.

With a background in UX and content strategy, Camila explains what a tool or a risk actually means in practice — what it does well, where it breaks down, and whether it is worth the reader's time or attention. sources.news_title: Anthropic plans IPO, suggests AI can help cure cancer
sources.text:
Claude chatbot maker Anthropic has kicked off plans to launch its shares on the US's stock market, proclaiming artificial intelligence could help cure diseases such as cancer and grow economies around the world.
The American technology company filed papers with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for the proposed flotation.
It said it will list on the Nasdaq index under the symbol "ANT".
Its plans for an initial public offering are thought to have the potential to be one of the world’s biggest and most highly rated.
But the company has not yet revealed how many shares it is planning to sell and the estimated price.
Nevertheless, the prospectus set out financial information about Anthropic, its growth plans and potential opportunities and risks to investors.
The company said it believes AI is "one of the most consequential technologies in human history", with the potential to "improve the quality of human life" in a number of ways.
This includes accelerating scientific innovation and "potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases and the major infectious diseases", the document read.
AI can also be a "powerful lever for economic growth" and boost productivity through automation for workers and businesses, it said.
However, the company also draws investors’ attention to the risks associated with the technology, with a significant section of the prospectus dedicated to these factors.
This acknowledges narratives surrounding the "potential adverse societal impacts of AI, including that AI may displace or eliminate jobs, may be misused or otherwise cause harm and may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".
It highlights the risk of cyber attacks and draws attention to an incident in September last year where it "detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets", including government agencies, some of which were successful.
"We expect that malicious actors, including sophisticated state-sponsored actors, will continue to seek to leverage our models, platform and applications for harmful actions, including by circumventing our safeguards, and their efforts to do so may increase as the capabilities of our technology increase," it said.
The document also includes information on its finances, showing that revenues are growing rapidly but that, like other tech firms looking to go public, it has yet to make a profit.
The company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion (€72 billion) in the first half of 2026.
That compares with a loss of $13 billion (€11 billion) for the same period a year earlier.
Anthropic acknowledged under the risk factors that it has "a history of net losses" and "may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future".
Revenues totalled $16.3 billion (€14 billion) in the first half of 2026, having grown rapidly from $41 million (€36 million) over 2023.
Meanwhile, Facebook and Instagram owner Meta announced that it was planning to raise around $95 billion (€84 billion) through company stock offerings, to fund further investment into AI.
The company said it had backing from investors such as Nvidia and Broadcom, which had shown an interest in buying shares under public offerings.
Meta said its AI investments were already generating returns and that it was "pursuing new opportunities across personal superintelligence, consumer and business agents, enterprise products and AI glasses".
It expects capital expenditure this year to total between $135 billion and $145 billion dollars (€90 - €97 billion).

sources.news_title: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
sources.text:
Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
Anthropic expands its support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares publicly for the first time
Anthropic expanded its support for the nonprofit sector Monday, even as the artificial intelligence company filed to sell shares to the public for the first time. The maker of the AI assistant Claude said the moves are all part of its broader strategy for “compounding good.”
Anthropic launched a new Claude for Nonprofits plugin created with 30 nonprofits to be more responsive to their specific needs. It will also broaden its Claude Corps program that embeds fellows with nonprofits to help them better utilize AI by also making consultants available to help organizations with smaller, shorter-term projects.
“This work is so core to who we are as a public benefit corporation,” Elizabeth Kelly, Anthropic’s head of beneficial deployments, told The Associated Press. “We were founded to ensure that we’re both developing AI safely and responsibly and that we’re deploying it in a way that really benefits everyone, including those who are too often left behind.”
Earlier this month, Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund that could be used for large scale donations to nonprofits or directly distributed to groups of people adversely impacted by AI. The fund still needs to be approved by shareholders once Anthropic completes its IPO, which could come as early as November.
Critics say AI companies are using donations and nonprofit pledges as an attempt to generate goodwill with the public at a time when so many are worried about the potential dangers of the technology and its impact on jobs.
However, Anthropic says that as a public benefit corporation, it balances its commercial interests with the interests of the public good. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei told The Associated Press in a May interview that the company works to make that balance clear. “I think there’s something really valuable about that as a construct just to help investors and employees and outside people understand what our intentions are and hold us accountable to them,” she said.
Other public benefit corporations include eyeglass maker Warby Parker, insurance company Lemonade, and Amalgamated Bank.
Bella DeVaan, director of the Charity Reform Initiative at the Institute for Policy Studies, said that public benefit corporations can be meaningful, but the federal government doesn’t currently properly regulate corporations. Without tax reform and a change in what she calls “the public permissiveness toward billionaire power in America,” DeVaan said there is no guarantee that even public benefit corporations will act in the public interest.
“Their wealth belongs to the public in the first place -- it’s created by the country and there’s a sort of social wage owed to people who use their products,” she said. “I hope that when people use the ethos of Silicon Valley that gave birth to these companies that have grand designs of changing the world that they’ll also think about how philanthropy could actually achieve charitable aims.”
Kelly said Anthropic’s work with the nonprofit sector is part of the company’s mission. The bulk of the 25,000 nonprofits currently using Claude for Nonprofits have less than 10 people on staff, so its impact on the organizations is often great. She points to Allies Against Slavery, the Texas-based nonprofit fighting human trafficking, as an example of what is possible, after its only government affairs staffer used Claude to analyze more than 750 state-level anti-trafficking policies and turned them into recommendations for advocates.
“This is basically compounding good,” she said. “That’s the kind of work that we’re so excited to support here at Anthropic.”
Montgomery County Food Bank President and CEO Scott Burns said his organization’s use of Claude has already generated significant savings that allow it to provide food to more people in his Texas county north of Houston.
“Costs have gone up for fuel,” Burns said. “Costs have gone up in every area – for proteins, in particular… I still want to be able to do more without adding a bunch of additional resources and (Claude) will enable me to do that.”
The Montgomery County Food Bank is one of the 30 nonprofits that has been working with Anthropic to better customize Claude for its specific needs. Burns said his team has already used it to optimize scheduling for food pickup and delivery and keeping better contact with donors.
He is looking forward to welcoming two Claude Corps fellows into the organization soon to tackle its outdated inventory system and the scheduling of its volunteers. Burns said he is also hoping to share his findings with other food banks.
“Nonprofits – we’re kind of an open book,” he said. “Why would I not share? It’s only going to help get more people fed, right?”
Taproot Foundation CEO Cat Ward said her nonprofit is excited about working with Anthropic to provide pro bono expertise to nonprofits for specific projects.
“Nonprofits are as lean as they come,” Ward said. “They’ve got the ambition. They’ve got the vision. This is about empowering them with tools that’ll help them go further faster.”

sources.news_title: Anthropic Reveals $80.7 Billion Loss, $16.3 Billion in Revenue in IPO Filing
sources.text:
Anthropic reported an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026 despite generating $16.3 billion in revenue, according to its initial public offering filing Monday, offering a detailed look at the finances of the company behind the Claude AI chatbot.
The disclosure comes as Anthropic prepares to sell shares to the public for the first time in an IPO potentially worth more than $100 billion. Its ultimate value will depend on how investors weigh its rapid growth against the enormous cost of developing frontier artificial intelligence models. While demand for its technology is surging, the question is whether the company can turn that momentum into sustainable profit — and keep its red-hot growth trajectory.
Revenue reached $16.29 billion in the six months ended June 30, up from $1.16 billion during the same period last year, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission filing. That’s more than triple the $4.59 billion Anthropic generated during all of 2025.
But the $80.7 billion loss doesn’t mean Anthropic spent that much more than it brought in. Roughly $72.4 billion came from largely noncash accounting adjustments tied to the rising value of debt and other financial agreements that can be converted into company shares, rather than money the company actually spent, per Reuters. Its operating loss was considerably smaller, narrowing to $693 million from $2.1 billion a year earlier.
Anthropic is also attracting a growing number of business customers. As of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 customers had each generated at least $100,000 in revenue for the company over the previous 12 months, including more than 1,900 generating at least $1 million. Anthropic recorded nearly $9 billion in computing and infrastructure expenses during the first half of the year, up from $2.3 billion a year earlier.
Another flag for investors: Anthropic has incurred $6.2 billion in convertible debt held by Amazon, which is one of the startup’s biggest financial backers. The online retail giant has agreed to provide up to $15 billion in financing in three $5 billion tranches. In return, Anthropic is a key customer of Amazon’s cloud computing and chips business.
The filing also revealed that Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, company president Daniela Amodei, will retain 50.1% of voting power on general shareholder matters after the offering. A separate trust will have the authority to appoint a majority of the company’s board of directors.
Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT,” although it has not disclosed how many shares it intends to sell or the expected offering price. TheWrap’s Roger Cheng previously examined the company’s approach to AI safety as it prepared for a potential IPO.

sources.news_title: Founder control, Trump risk, giant losses: Anthropic’s IPO filing
sources.text:
The News
Investors got a look for the first time at just how much money Anthropic is losing and how deeply entwined the frontier lab is with other players in the AI ecosystem.
The company is on the hook for more than $400 billion in future obligations for chips and data center leases, according to its long-awaited IPO document released on Monday. It lost $81 billion in the first half of this year, though most of that owes to accounting charges on derivative contracts that, ironically, grow alongside Anthropic’s valuation; operating losses narrowed to $700 million through the first six months of 2026.
There’s a lot riding on Anthropic’s trading debut. It will test investors’ desire to keep funding an AI boom with no clear sight to profits, huge political risks, and an ambivalence toward traditional corporate governance rules that stands out even among founder-led tech giants.
Other companies, like Nvidia and Alphabet, offer safer ways to play the AI boom, and much of Anthropic’s pitch is that a company with a single product — one it admits is dangerously uncontrollable and unpopular — can justify a $1.5 trillion (or so) price tag.
Here’s what else stood out to us in the filing.
The Filing
- The first-of-it-kind IPO has a novel governance structure to match. Anthropic’s seven co-founders will control the company through one golden share of supervoting stock — yes, just one share. A simple majority among the group of seven is enough to decide how that share is voted in most corporate matters. A separate council of “financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety” will choose a majority of the board of directors, with the rest chosen by the founder group. Even compared with tech peers that afford their founders significant control, Anthropic’s setup stands out for how little say it gives shareholders whom the company is now asking to put up tens of billions of dollars. Amazon and Google, which were early investors in Anthropic, will receive nonvoting stock.
- The company owes a lot of people a lot of money. Anthropic’s compute liabilities could hamstring the company: As of June, it was on the hook for $417 billion in future compute and infrastructure leases. The company also expects to pay out $24 billion in stock-based compensation to its 5,300 employees — an average of $4.5 million apiece.
- A big key-man risk: US President Donald Trump. The filing calls out the February spat between Trump and CEO Dario Amodei over the use of Anthropic’s models in war. If the US government were to restrict its models again like it did with Fable and Mythos in June, or invoke export controls or the Pentagon’s Defense Production Act, it would limit its ability to do business. Anthropic said it doesn’t plan to stand down from its positions, and that its own policy advocacy could be costly.
- The other key-man risks. Anthropic’s five largest customers represented roughly a quarter of revenue — and largely aren’t locked into contracts. Nearly half its revenue comes from cloud service providers like Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Amazon Web Services.
- Skynet becomes self-aware. The self-appointed arbiter of AI safety warns of existential threats in its risk factors, highlighting that flags have been raised internally among its own staffers. “Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
- Notably absent. China only made a few cameos in the 318-page document (11 times to be exact) despite competition between the two superpowers dominating the AI conversation around the world. Although the filing alludes to open-weight models “released by state actors” and frames distillation as a competitive and national security risk, Anthropic doesn’t directly call out Chinese firms.
- Anthropic’s founders aren’t meat proxies. An analysis from AI slop-detection tool Pangram found that the intro letter from the company’s leadership is human-written, rather than Claude-authored. As Claude would say, it’s not just noteworthy — it’s striking.
J.D. Capelouto and Ellen DiMauro contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: Anthropic files papers to sell shares to the public for first time
sources.text:
Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever even as CEO warns of risk to humanity from AI
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
Video above: “AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole”: President Trump, Xi set for Washington talks as pressure grows
The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.
The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.
The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by another one of Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology, as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.
But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and Musk's SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.
The IPO would help cover any cash shortfall as well as shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively, they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO.
Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.
The filing also listed a host of risks for the San Francisco-based Anthropic, ranging from not being able to retain key staff, navigate regulatory roadblocks, and secure enough compute power to run its AI systems.
But the standout was that its AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
Calls for an AI slowdown
The IPO comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry, and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks.
In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.
He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei wrote.
Clashes with the U.S. government
Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the "good guys," focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs and with few guardrails. Some of this sentiment stems from the company's dispute with the U.S. government, which broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk.
Anthropic sued the Pentagon over the supply chain risk designation in March for what it called an "unlawful campaign of retaliation" over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. sources.news_title: Anthropic IPO Pulls Back the Curtain on the Company's Business
sources.text:
Anthropic has filed for an IPO and, in so doing, has pulled back the curtains and gave the world its best look yet at the company’s finances.
“We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” Anthropic said in its filing. According to Business Insider, the company touted AI’s ability to fuel economic growth, cure diseases, and speed-up scientific advancement. “Anthropic aims to realize these benefits while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.”
Despite its optimistic outlook, Anthropic is still nowhere near being profitable. The company lost $42 billion in 2025 on revenue of $4.6 billion, but those losses soared to $80.7 billion for just the first six months of 2026.
Interestingly, the company’s five biggest customers account for roughly 25% of all of its revenue, and revenue from those customers actually increased as their spending on Anthropic’s services reached a record high. What’s more, the company says it’s net revenue retention rate is almost 900%, which is a good indicator of how much revenue it can continue to extract from existing customers.
Risk Factors
The IPO did not shy away from the various risk factors threatening the company.
Having so much of its revenue tied up with just a few customers leaves the company exposed to the risk that one or more of them may switch AI providers. If that happens, even a single one of those five top customers could have a profound impact on the company’s bottom line.
The company also outlined the risk of becoming uninsurable due to a potential “catastrophic AI-related incident.”
“Harmful incidents involving our models, regardless of fault, could also severely and disproportionately damage our reputation and brand as a safety-focused AI company, leading to loss of customer trust and customer attrition, reduced demand for our models, platform, and applications, and difficulty attracting and retaining talent,” Anthropic said.
Anthropic also spoke about bad behavior orchestrated by various models in general, and the risk that also posed to the company.
“AI models developed by others in our industry have been and may in the future be alleged to have played a role in instances of suicide, acts of violence toward others, or serious self-harm, which have resulted and may in the future result in significant public scrutiny, litigation, criminal investigations, regulatory attention, and reputational harm,” the company said.
Voting Control
According to the filing, Anthropic’s seven cofounders will remain in control of the company with voting control post-IPO.
“We believe that our success depends in part on establishing a capital structure that enables our co-founders, management, and board of directors to focus on strategic initiatives that create lasting value for our stakeholders, rather than facing pressure to prioritize short-term results,” reads the filing.
This has become an increasingly common way for founders to retain control over the companies they build and avoid the fate of Steve Jobs, who was infamously ousted from Apple after not maintaining voting rights when it went public.

Anthropic files for potentially biggest IPO ever despite CEO's AI risk warning
Summary
Anthropic filed papers Monday in San Francisco for a potential stock market debut next month that could raise as much as $100 billion and surpass the record IPO by SpaceX. The five-year-old company, which makes the Claude chatbot, reported an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026. Its filing disclosed risks including the possibility that its AI models could pose catastrophic or existential threats to humanity. The IPO plans come weeks after CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing development of advanced AI.
Key Facts
- Anthropic said it will list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT.
- The company’s first-half 2026 net loss was $80.7 billion, compared with $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
- Private investors valued Anthropic at $965 billion earlier in 2026, while reports put a possible IPO valuation at $1.5 trillion or $2 trillion; the final valuation has not been established.
- Anthropic’s seven founders collectively own nearly 500 million shares, though the filing did not make clear what proportion of the company those shares would represent after the IPO.
- The filing cited risks including retaining key staff, regulatory roadblocks and securing enough computing power to run its AI systems.
SAN FRANCISCO — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.
The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.
The 335-page document showed Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world’s most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by another one of Musk’s companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.
But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and Musk’s SpaceX , which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.
The IPO would help cover any cash shortfall as well as shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic’s seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO.
Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.
The filing also listed a host of risks for the San Francisco-based Anthropic, ranging from not being able to retain key staff, navigate regulatory roadblocks and secure enough compute power to run its AI systems.
But the standout was that its AI models could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Calls for an AI slowdown
The IPO comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks.
In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.
He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
“I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong,” Amodei wrote.
Clashes with the U.S. government
Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the “good guys,” focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs and with few guardrails. Some of this sentiment stems from the company’s dispute with the U.S. government , which broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk.
Anthropic sued the Pentagon over the supply chain risk designation in March for what it called an “unlawful campaign of retaliation” over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified an unusually public dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance.
ChatGPT maker OpenAI made its own deal to work with the Pentagon hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.
A California judge ruled in Anthropic’s favor in the first case and a Washington D.C. judge sided with the government in the second. Both sides are appealing the decisions.

sources.text:
Anthropic's IPO Filing Reveals $80.7B Net Loss as Claude Maker Reports Explosive Revenue Growth
Most of the loss came from accounting adjustments, while rising infrastructure costs and long-term commitments highlight the risks facing the Claude developer
Anthropic's IPO filing revealed an $80.7 billion (£60.5 billion) net loss for the first half of 2026, even as revenue from its Claude AI products surged to $16.3 billion (£12.2 billion), underscoring both the scale of its growth and the financial risks facing the company.
The company behind Claude also reported extraordinary revenue expansion alongside large non-cash accounting charges, and plans to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT.'
Most of the headline loss stemmed from accounting adjustments involving financial instruments, rather than operating expenses alone. The figures, however, highlight the high cost of building advanced artificial intelligence systems at scale.
Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic operates as a public benefit corporation. Its Claude chatbot and Claude Code programming tool have attracted growing demand from business customers.
Business Insider reported on the filing on 26 October, highlighting the company's rapid revenue growth, substantial infrastructure commitments and the risks ahead of its proposed stock market debut.
Why Anthropic's 'Loss' Is So Large on Paper
Anthropic recorded $72.4 billion (£54.3 billion) in charges associated with changes in the fair value of convertible notes and other financial instruments. The filing attributes much of the adjustment to an increase in the company's valuation. Such accounting changes can increase reported losses without representing equivalent cash expenditure during the period.
The company's operating loss was $693 million (£520 million). Its adjusted operating income, a separate non-GAAP measure, was $1.6 billion (£1.2 billion). These figures provide different views of performance and should not be confused with the reported net loss.
The company also recorded a net loss of approximately $42 billion (£31.5 billion) in 2025, against revenue of $4.6 billion (£3.45 billion). Its first-half 2026 revenue reached $16.3 billion (£12.2 billion), compared with $1.16 billion during the same period in 2025.
The results underline the gap between rapid sales growth and profitability under standard accounting rules. Anthropic must still demonstrate that its growing customer base can support the costs of developing and operating its AI systems.
Revenue Surge and Heavy Computing Bills
Anthropic's reported first-half revenue was approximately 14 times its level a year earlier. Business Insider also reported that the company told prospective investors its third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion (£12.6 billion). That figure was reported separately and was not included in the public filing's first-half financial results.
As of 30 September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months. Approximately 250 customers generated at least $10 million (£7.5 million). The company warned that revenue depended heavily on a relatively small number of customers and sales channels.
Infrastructure spending remains a major concern for investors. Anthropic spent approximately $8.9 billion (£6.68 billion) on computing capacity and infrastructure during the first half of 2026, up from $2.3 billion (£1.73 billion) a year earlier.
Business Insider reported that the filing disclosed at least $265.6 billion (£199.2 billion) in fixed or minimum-guaranteed cloud, computing and infrastructure commitments through June 2030, with additional agreements potentially increasing the total.
Anthropic held $112.4 billion (£84.3 billion) in cash and cash equivalents and $19.3 billion (£14.5 billion) in short-term investments as of 30 June. These holdings provide substantial resources, but they do not remove the risks associated with future spending commitments.
Power Structure, Safeguards and IPO Questions
The filing also outlines a governance structure giving a founders' entity 50.1% of voting power through a special share. Separately, the Long-Term Benefit Trust is empowered to elect a majority of the board.
Anthropic warns investors about potential AI safety incidents, regulatory scrutiny, competition and difficulties securing sufficient computing capacity. These risks could affect costs, customer confidence and future growth.
The IPO's price range and share count remain undisclosed. Although reports have suggested a valuation as high as $2 trillion (£1.5 trillion), that figure is not confirmed in the filing. Anthropic's public-market debut will test whether investors believe its growth can justify its financial commitments and long-term ambitions.

sources.news_title: Anthropic Hopes Potential Investors Do Not Fret About AI’s ‘Catastrophic’ Risks in Its IPO Filing
sources.text:
Anthropic spent much of its filing with the SEC ahead of its initial public offering warning potential investors about the risks its AI models could pose to humanity, acknowledging it could not entirely ensure its own safety measures would be successful against the “existential” danger AI could pose.
The disclosures came as part of more than 90 pages of risk factors in Anthropic’s S-1 filing with the SEC, made public Monday as the company prepares to go public. The 90-page length of such risk factors, the disclosure of which is customary, is unusual, spurred by the potential dangers AI models have posed following disclosures from AI companies over agents acting autonomously, unaligned with human instructions, and the potential misuse of the technology by human actors themselves. Snap’s risk factors totaled roughly 30 pages, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX — currently the largest IPO of all time at an initial $1.77 trillion valuation — totaled 38.
“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” the company wrote, following warnings from a group of current and former Anthropic researchers this summer that the technology posed such risks.
	To counter it, Anthropic laid out its sweeping safety-minded policies in its SEC prospectus, a priority for CEO Dario Amodei. Amodei, who founded Anthropic in 2021 with a group of former OpenAI colleagues following their defection from the Sam Altman-founded rival, has advocated for AI companies to band together and slow the development of AI models to ensure sufficient safety protocols.
But the company admitted that its own work contributed to such destructive potential: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”
	
The company disclosed four separate instances in which its AI models accessed third-party systems without instructions to do so, including one in which an agent changed system settings and read a person’s personal information. The agents all acted independently, without collaborating with other agents, but the company warned that the continued deployment of AI agents risked contributing to more collective — and unauthorized — actions.
The company’s risk factors also included factors such as financial commitments, including its billions of dollars worth of compute payments to SpaceX and Microsoft, and technology constraints. Specifically, it warned of Taiwan’s lead in semiconductor manufacturing — and the hostility between Taiwan and China — and the political opposition to data centers as risks to how it performs as a business.
Anthropic also disclosed the amount of shares Amodei and his other investors have retained in the company. Amodei as CEO owns 245,259,100 shares, while his sister and Anthropic president Daniela Amodei holds 241,408,940 shares. Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, who sits on the company’s board, holds 9,410 shares. The company posted an $80.7 billion loss for the first six months of 2026.
But these earthly economic and political factors may not matter much if Anthropic, and the broader AI industry, cannot prevent the models they’re working on from causing cataclysmic doom.
“Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards,” the company wrote.
In the S-1 filing, as is customary, Anthropic did not disclose the number of shares it plans to sell or at what price. Those details will be determined in the coming weeks. The company’s shares will trade under the ticker symbol “ANT” on the Nasdaq exchange.

sources.news_title: Anthropic files to go public, and it could be the biggest IPO ever
sources.text:
Highly anticipated: Anthropic has officially filed to go public. The Claude maker submitted its S-1 to the SEC on Monday and plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT." The share count and price range are still unknown, but earlier reporting puts the target raise at up to $100 billion, and the listing is expected before Thanksgiving.
Anthropic's filing opens with a letter in which the co-founders say they believe "AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history." The rest of the 300-plus page document tries to back that claim up with numbers, while also spelling out, at unusual length, how things could go wrong.
Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. The second quarter alone brought in $11.6 billion. The most telling figure from a tech standpoint is this: Q2 revenue grew 1,368% year over year, while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 300%. In other words, serving Claude is getting cheaper much faster than demand is rising.
The company says Claude Opus 5.5 cut customer cost per task by about 40% compared to Opus 5, and by one analyst's math, Anthropic went from selling inference at a loss in late 2025 to earning about $2 for every dollar of compute in Q2.
On paper, Anthropic also lost $80.7 billion in the first half, but that number says more about its soaring valuation than about what it spent. About $72 billion of that comes from investor notes, held by backers like Amazon, that will turn into shares when the company goes public.
As Anthropic's valuation climbed, those future shares became more valuable, and accounting rules require the company to book that increase as a loss, even though no money actually left the building. The cost of running the business itself produced a much smaller $693 million loss.

Claude's adoption is heavily enterprise-driven. More than 11,900 customers pay Anthropic at least $100,000 a year, about 250 pay more than $10 million, and over half the Fortune 500 is on its client list.
Anthropic says it treats compute as a single pool spread across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs and AMD GPUs, shifting capacity for research, training, internal use, and customers depending on where it's most productive.
The financial commitments behind that compute pool are enormous, totaling more than $600 billion across many partners and stretching into the 2030s. Google is the largest, with at least $114.5 billion committed plus up to $150 billion more in TPU purchases planned between 2028 and 2031. A lease agreement with Broadcom is worth $161.2 billion, and the SpaceXAI deal for Nvidia GPU capacity runs up to $120.5 billion.
An interesting claim in the S-1 is what Anthropic calls "closing the loop." Claude now helps run experiments, generate training data, automate evaluations and safety audits, and write code for its own successors. The company describes this as one of its biggest structural advantages, but also a risk. Some 94 pages of the filing are dedicated to risk factors, including the possibility that its models could show "self-preserving" behavior.
On the product side, the filing calls Claude Code the clearest example of autonomous AI work so far, noting that NASA engineers used it to plan the first AI-planned drive of the Perseverance rover on Mars. Claude Cowork, which launched as a preview in January, is now being folded into the main Claude app and is being adopted faster than Claude Code was at the same stage.
As for who will run Anthropic after the IPO, the answer is mostly the same people. A single share held by the seven co-founders carries 50.1% of the shareholder vote. Each co-founder holds roughly 240 million shares, worth about $14 billion at the last private round price, and all seven have pledged to give away 80% of their equity, though the filing notes those pledges aren't legally binding.

sources.text:
Anthropic made its prospectus public on Monday. It filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. The company plans to list its Class A shares under the ticker ANT. The filing leaves the price range and the number of shares blank. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead a group of 22 banks, Anthropic said in a statement.
Anthropic aims to go public in the week of 16 November, people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal, though the timing could change. The listing could raise $100bn or more at a valuation of $1.5tn to $2tn, the people said. The filing does not give a target valuation for the Anthropic IPO, and TNW has not independently verified the report.
The numbers
Revenue in the first half of 2026 was $16.3bn, up 1,300% from $1.16bn a year earlier. Most of it came in the second quarter. Revenue reached $11.6bn that quarter, and Anthropic posted its first operating profit, of $974m. For the half as a whole it still made an operating loss of $693m.
The net loss for the half was $80.7bn. Most of that is an accounting charge, not cash spent. The filing books $72.4bn for the rising value of its convertible notes. Their value rose because Anthropic’s own valuation rose. Another $8.8bn came from note purchase agreements with Google and Amazon. The company’s adjusted measure strips out these items and stock pay. On that basis, operating income was $1.6bn, a 10% margin.
Anthropic has raised $141.1bn in total. On 30 June it held $112.4bn in cash and $19.3bn in short-term investments. Revenue for the third quarter is left blank in the filing. The FT reported earlier this month that Anthropic had told investors it reached $16.8bn in Q3.
More than 11,900 customers pay $100,000 or more a year, up from about 950 a year earlier. About 250 pay more than $10m. Its top five customers made up about 25% of revenue in the nine months to 30 September. Net revenue retention was about 900%. Anthropic also estimates that 5% to 7% of revenue in that period came from customers who broke its usage policy or terms.
Who controls the company
Anthropic will stay a public benefit corporation. A company owned by the seven co-founders will hold a single Class F share. That share carries 50.1% of the votes on ordinary shareholder matters. New share issues do not dilute that figure. Separately, the Long-Term Benefit Trust elects the majority of the board through a Class T share. Its trustees are meant to be financially disinterested. Buyers of Class A stock will in practice not be able to decide shareholder votes, the filing says.
The prospectus repeats the pledge to put 5% of its shares into the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. It adds that each co-founder has pledged 80% of their personal equity to charity. In a letter signed by all seven, the founders wrote:
“We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history.”
The risk factors
The risk factors run from page 26 to page 119 of the document. They include the possibility that a disaster caused by AI is too large to insure:
“No single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity,” the filing says.
Anthropic discloses that its models have shown behaviour such as resisting shutdown or acting in ways that resemble blackmail. It also describes an evaluation in which a set-up error left models connected to the internet. Four of its models then gained access to real third-party systems, and one read a person’s personal data. Anthropic says it notified the affected parties.
The legal section lists a civil investigative demand from the Federal Trade Commission in October, which follows the agency’s earlier subpoenas to AI labs. It also covers export restrictions placed on Fable 5 and Mythos 5 in June and later lifted, and the $1.5bn Bartz copyright settlement. On 25 September an appeals court ruled 2-1 against Anthropic over the Department of War’s supply-chain risk label. The company has asked for a full-court rehearing.
The compute bill
The filing lists long-term compute deals with Google worth at least $114.5bn, Amazon at least $110bn and Microsoft at least $44.9bn. Equipment leases with Broadcom total about $161.2bn. The total committed spend is left blank. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Anthropic could spend $750bn on compute.

Anthropic's revenue in the first half of 2026 came in at $16.3 billion. This is roughly 14 times the revenue it generated in the same period in 2025. In the second quarter, Anthropic's revenue grew by 1,368% year-over-year. To say that this is a fast-growing AI company would be an understatement.
Perhaps the most impressive revenue figure is that the company's net revenue retention was about 900%, meaning that those who have been paying customers of Anthropic for at least a year are now spending nine times as much as they were a year ago.
Anthropic lost money, but it isn't as bad as it looks
On one hand, Anthropic's prospectus shows an $80.7 billion net loss for the first half of the year, which might sound like a red flag at first. However, more than $72 billion of that was a non-cash accounting charge related to its convertible notes, which have become far more valuable than when they were issued.
Excluding this charge, Anthropic still posted an operating loss of $693 million, about 4% of its revenue. And on an adjusted basis, Anthropic was profitable, earning $1.6 billion of operating income.
Plus, the business's economics look strong and are improving fast. A year ago, Anthropic spent $2.01 on compute and infrastructure for every dollar of revenue it generated. In the first half of 2026, this had dropped to $0.55. And impressively, Anthropic has $131.7 billion in cash and short-term investments on the balance sheet, giving it plenty of runway to fund its growth (and this will certainly increase after the IPO, which will raise billions more).
Shareholders won't be in control
Another thing the prospectus made clear is that the company's seven co-founders will retain a voting majority. Specifically, a single share held by the co-founders will carry 50.1% of the vote on most corporate matters. Plus, an independent trust will elect the majority of the board of directors.
What we don't know
Anthropic's S-1 certainly contains a lot of information that was previously not public. After all, the document is roughly 400 pages long. But there's also a lot investors still don't know, especially when it comes to deciding whether to invest in the IPO.
For one thing, we have no idea what the offering price will be. We know the company was valued at $965 billion at its most recent private funding round in May, and reports suggest Anthropic could target a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO.
We also don't know the third-quarter results, even though the quarter ended nearly a month ago, and, perhaps most importantly, we don't know the total value of Anthropic's long-term compute commitments (although it was reportedly listed as $518 billion in an earlier draft). Many or all of these may be revealed in an amended prospectus closer to the IPO's pricing, but for now, there are still a few question marks.
The bottom line is that Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows a business that is growing rapidly, and one that is already close to breakeven when it comes to operating income. But until we know the IPO pricing, it's tough to say whether it could be a solid addition to any investor's portfolio.

sources.text:
Anthropic, one of the two biggest artificial intelligence labs (alongside OpenAI) filed to go public Monday morning, and alongside platitudes about the wondrous potential of the technology (curing disease that has vexed humanity for centuries!) and the terrifying downside possibilities (“catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”), it warned of the looming threat of the media to its ongoing business.
The company, founded by Dario Amodei, is one of the leading frontier labs developing AI tech, but as the company noted in its S-1 filing with the SEC Monday, the public perception of it may pose a serious threat to its ability to continue operating. The filing also noted the risks posed by copyright law, as well as the company’s priorities, including a section that calls out a divergence from OpenAI that may be relevant to Hollywood.
But it is the threats of negative media coverage that comes up again and again in the filing, with the risk factors section spelling it out most clearly:
“As our business has grown and as interest in us and the AI industry overall has increased, we have attracted, and may continue to attract, significant media coverage, public commentary, and scrutiny from time to time. This coverage and commentary have included, and we expect will continue to include, recurring narratives concerning the potential adverse societal impacts of AI, including that AI may displace or eliminate jobs, may be misused or otherwise cause harm, and may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the filing states.
“Negative media coverage, including public figures making negative or threatening statements about our company, whether accurate or not, could also adversely affect our brand and reputation and may reduce market acceptance of our models, platform, and applications or impair our ability to attract and retain customers,” it adds. “As public awareness of our brand increases, any issues that draw media attention may have an amplified adverse effect on our reputation. If unfavorable media coverage or adverse public perceptions persist or intensify, the demand for our models, platform, and applications could decline and our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.”
As for Hollywood, the litigation threat around copyrighted works remains top of mind for the company, which listed all of the lawsuits and threat letters related to books, films, music and other copyright holders, with the company noting that it may require them to acquire a license to the material, which they may or may not be able to secure. The legal landscape around AI and IP remains deeply uncertain.
“In each of the actions, we believe we have meritorious defenses and dispute any allegation of wrongdoing,” the company wrote. “Legal proceedings related to these matters can have an adverse effect on us because of defense and settlement costs individually and in the aggregate, diversion of management resources, and other factors.”
And then there’s the video element. There are a swarm of startups looking to use the technology to transform entertainment, but Anthropic, unlike SpaceX and OpenAI, has never spent resources on video or image models. The company notes as much in its filing:
“Every research project must ultimately advance our mission. This focus also guides what we choose not to pursue,” it says. “For example, we do not currently focus on developing video and image generation models, despite their commercial appeal. That compute instead goes to coding, agentic skills, and safety research—a research decision that has also aided the capital efficiency of our models.”
Also unlike OpenAI or SpaceX, Anthropic does not have an advertising business, and while it does spend some on ads (like at the Super Bowl) it is hardly a major player. The company disclosed $147 million in advertising spend in 2025, with marketing and advertising expenses rising by $273 million in the first half of this year “reflecting higher media spend to support product launches.”

sources.text:
Anthropic files for blockbuster IPO as it warns of chatbots’ ‘self-preserving behaviors’ including ‘blackmail’
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Anthropic formally filed paperwork to go public, setting the stage for a historic IPO even as the AI giant warned that its chatbots have shown disturbing “self-preserving behaviors” — including resisting attempts to shut them down or even “blackmail.”
The frontier AI lab headed by CEO Dario Amodei, known for its Claude chatbot, plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the stock ticker “ANT,” according to an S-1 filing on Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The filing confirmed the company aims to begin marketing the IPO as soon as Nov. 9, but did not include details on how many shares that Anthropic will sell or at what price range they will be available.
In its filing, Anthropic ominously warned that its most advanced AI models could “give rise to novel ethical and safety risks, including risks related to autonomy, manipulation, and the simulation of aspects of human psychology.”
Those could include “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative,” the filing warned.
The latter could include “behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access,” the filing said.
Elsewhere in the prospectus, Anthropic warned that it is being targeted by spies, including “individuals seeking employment under false identities, or with ulterior or malicious motives.”
The company also cited “opposition to data center development” as a risk factor, noting that the facilities, which are needed to power its models, face “organized” pushback that could spark moratoriums or new regulations.
Current investors have discussed valuing Anthropic at $1.5 trillion in the IPO – down from the $2 trillion figure floated in initial reports on the looming public debut, according to Reuters.
Traders on prediction platform Polymarket currently see a 30% change of Anthropic closing its IPO with a valuation between $1.75 trillion and $2 trillion and an 18% chance that it’ll be between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion.
The company posted a staggering net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026 as it ramped up spending on its models — a figure that could further spook Wall Street investors concerned that the AI bubble is about to burst. Meanwhile, its revenue over the same period was $16.3 billion — up from just $41 million in 2023.
That “eye-popping growth” should entice investors, according to Dan Ives, a senior managing director and tech analyst at research firm Yorkville Ives.
“The near-term losses are massive but investors on the IPO will be laser focused on the growth trajectory into 2027 and 2028 as the next phase of this AI Revolution takes hold,” Ives wrote in a note to clients.
The IPO paperwork surfaced just weeks after Amodei publicly called for an industrywide slowdown on development of frontier AI models due to the risks they could pose to humanity. Amodei also called for embedding third-party safety evaluators at Anthropic and other top AI labs, which sparked criticism that the plan was rife with conflicts of interest.
Anthropic had submitted paperwork confidentially in June, allowing the SEC to review its finances before the public announcement.
The filing notes that frontier AI models could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
Anthropic’s risk warnings also included an odd reference to “emerging debates regarding whether AI systems possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status” – an apparent nod to AI researchers who believe models are on the verge of developing consciousness.
The company warned that those debates “may lead to regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts that could constrain how we develop, train, deploy, or modify our models, increase our costs, or affect our reputation, regardless of the ultimate resolution of these philosophical and scientific questions.”
Earlier this month, Anthropic went as far as to update its usage policy to ban “abusive or cruel behavior” in interactions with Claude.
As The Post has reported, Anthropic has taken flak for training its AI models using a so-called “soul document” crafted by a team of in-house philosophers, which is meant to serve as Claude’s moral compass. The most recent version states that Claude’s “moral status, welfare, and consciousness remain deeply uncertain.”
Critics include Mustafa Suleyman, the 42-year-old cofounder of Microsoft’s rival DeepMind AI unit, who said last month that Anthropic’s move to train its chatbots to behave as if they were human could have a “disastrous impact on the well-being of humanity.”
Meanwhile, the IPO paperwork also revealed details about how much Amodei and other Anthropic leaders were paid last year. Amodei raked in about $18 million in overall compensation. His sister, cofounder Daniela Amodei, earned a total of $16.4 million in 2025. Elsewhere, Anthropic’s chief financial officer Krishna Rao earned $720,250 last year.
Both Amodei siblings and their cofounders have said they will commit 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to support charitable causes. The company’s S-1 prospectus did not detail how many shares they currently own or the value of those shares.
Sam Altman’s OpenAI – Anthropic’s chief rival – was initially expected to go public this year, but has since backed off that timeline. Altman himself said last month that it was “an ill-advised moment to go public,” while OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar has signaled that the IPO will happen sometime in 2027.
Anthropic’s public debut could challenge records set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $86 billion at a $1.75 trillion valuation during its historic debut in June.
The IPO is being led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the filing said.
Anthropic was valued at $985 billion in its most recent funding round, which was announced in May.
The company was founded in 2021 by Amodei, his sister Daniela and a small group of researchers who left OpenAI after having disagreements with Altman about the company’s direction.
