The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.
The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by another one of Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.
But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and Musk's SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.
The IPO would help cover any cash shortfall as well as shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively, they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO.
The filing also listed a host of risks for the San Francisco-based Anthropic, ranging from not being able to retain key staff, navigate regulatory roadblocks and secure enough compute power to run its AI systems.
But the standout was that its AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
The IPO comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks.
In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.
He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei wrote.

sources.text:
Updated October 26, 2026 at 4:37 PM PDT
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.
Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.
The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.
Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.
In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.
AI stocks have been hit by volatility
The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.
The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.
"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.
But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.
With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.
Concerns remain about the AI sector
The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.
Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.
The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.
Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.
Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.
In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

sources.news_title: Anthropic’s IPO S-1 Spells Out a Future of Promise and Peril
sources.text:
For years, Dario Amodei, a founder of the start-up Anthropic, has been painted as the pre-eminent doomsayer of artificial intelligence, often making sweeping statements about how the technology could wreak havoc on the world.
On Monday, as Dr. Amodei presented his company’s paperwork for what could be the biggest ever initial public offering on Wall Street, he painted a more nuanced picture: Even with its many risks, A.I. has the potential to bring about untold benefits to humanity.
From the very top of the founder’s letter — a kind of mission statement typical of many I.P.O. prospectuses — Dr. Amodei and his six co-founders set the stakes.
This is a view on which Dr. Amodei has long been consistent. Since Anthropic’s earliest days, he has argued that the technology has the capacity to profoundly change the world. Often, Dr. Amodei would harp on the negative consequences those changes may bring. Lately, he has more frequently been playing up some of the benefits.
It is in line with a change in tone Anthropic has recently pitched to its investors. Across the industry and even among Anthropic’s backers is a view that Dr. Amodei’s vocal concerns about the technology have overshadowed what many believe are its upsides — an important sales pitch as the company seeks to raise billions on the stock market.
In closed-door meetings, the company has said it plans to emphasize more of the positive aspects of A.I., from increased productivity for workers to curing the world’s worst ailments.
Anthropic is accused of focusing on economic disruption rather than benefit. Specifically, critics argue, the company more often stresses monumental job loss while peers focus on the many ways the technology will empower workers. In his letter, Dr. Amodei allows for a future of unprecedented growth, which could bring about worldwide prosperity.
He goes on to cite examples such as giving people access to the knowledge and skills of a lawyer, an accountant or a farmer.
And finally, Dr. Amodei notes that advancements in A.I. could unburden us from needless bureaucracy. He sketches a future where DMV lines are shortened, job seekers can receive services to find employment more easily and Medicaid systems are navigable. Perhaps most of all, he claims the technology can help “democratic governments deliver on their promises to citizens.”
Though the prospectus is front-loaded with sweetness and light, the paperwork has all the hallmarks of Anthropic’s anxieties. In page after page, the company lists the many risks that A.I. poses to its business — and society.
At least some of this is already happening. Over the summer, a series of cybersecurity breaches from Anthropic, OpenAI and other leading A.I. labs kicked off an industrywide discussion on how to safeguard advanced systems.
Dr. Amodei and the company go on to list the flip sides to all the positive possibilities laid out at the beginning of the document. With economic prosperity comes the potential for great upheaval.
And Anthropic suggests that just as democratic governments may be empowered, so too could autocratic regimes. Dr. Amodei continues:
No I.P.O. prospectus from Anthropic would have been complete without Dr. Amodei’s biggest concern, and what some might call the ultimate “risk factor” — a disclosure companies are required to make to investors about issues that could adversely affect their business.
Put more simply: Yes, Anthropic believes its technology could bring about conditions for human flourishing the likes of which have never been seen. The company also believes it could bring about the end of the world.
Most normal companies do not tend to address such weighty philosophical matters when filing to go public. But Anthropic is far from a normal company.

Anthropic opens its books for Wall Street, showing record revenue and mounting obligations
Key Points
- Anthropic filed its S-1 for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker "ANT."
- In Q2 2026, Anthropic pulled in $11.6 billion in revenue and posted its first GAAP operating profit at $974 million. The flip side: long-term compute commitments totaling $780 to $810 billion.
- Eighty percent of revenue comes from per-token billing based on actual usage. Existing customers are spending nine times more year over year on average.
Anthropic filed its IPO prospectus, and the market seems to like it.
The AI lab is the first major company of its kind to publicly file an S-1 with the SEC. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT," with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the offering. Wall Street expects a valuation of roughly $2 trillion, according to Yahoo Finance, up from the company's most recent private valuation of about $965 billion, which already put it ahead of rival OpenAI at roughly $852 billion.
The first-half numbers show huge growth. Revenue jumped from $376 million in Q1 2025 to $11.6 billion in Q2 2026, a 1,368 percent year-over-year increase. For the first half of 2026, Anthropic brought in $16.3 billion total, more than triple its full-year 2025 revenue of $4.6 billion. Government contracts account for only about one percent of that total, while roughly 5 to 7 percent comes from customers who violate usage policies, primarily through model distillation, which Anthropic has already been cracking down on.
In Q2 2026, Anthropic posted its first positive GAAP operating profit at $974 million. Compute costs rose 300 percent over the same period, but that's slower than revenue growth. Revenue per employee sits at $6.6 million, higher than any Magnificent 7 company except Nvidia, with about 5,300 people on staff. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD rallied after the filing went public.
Existing customers spend nine times more year over year
Anthropic's net revenue retention rate sits at roughly 900 percent, meaning existing customers are spending nine times what they did a year ago. That figure speaks to AI's scaling potential, especially considering most deployments are likely still shallow, depend on human oversight, and don't run AI at full speed yet.
More than 11,900 customers pay over $100,000 annually, and about 250 spend more than $10 million. No single customer accounts for more than ten percent of revenue, but five customers together make up 25 percent. If those include companies like Meta, Google, or Microsoft that could switch to their own or cheaper models, that concentration could become a risk.
Claude Enterprise users who also use Claude Code are the biggest spenders, paying about 20 times more than other customers, according to the S-1. Eighty percent of revenue is billed on actual usage, per token processed as the smallest billing unit for AI models, while the remaining 20 percent comes from fixed subscriptions. That split might signal how heavily subscriptions are still being cross-subsidized, but it also suggests Anthropic has room to raise prices. The company's forecast for next year will be primarily usage-based, according to the FT.
Compute commitments top $780 billion
Anthropic has taken on huge financial obligations to fuel its growth. Compute capacity contracts with Broadcom, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and other providers add up to roughly $780 to $810 billion, and those costs are more or less fixed and locked in long-term, while revenue remains variable and usage-dependent.
That means the company needs to keep growing fast to cover its future bills. If it can't, the AI-fueled capital market could start to wobble. To gain more flexibility and lower costs over time, Anthropic is building its own data centers under the name "Anthropic Direct".
Anthropic also left Q3 numbers out of the S-1, even though the company already has them. One possible reason is that growth slowed significantly in Q3. Momentum may have already picked back up, though. OpenRouter data shows demand for Anthropic models climbed again after the October release of the 5.5 series, especially Opus 5.5. OpenRouter only captures a tiny slice of total token demand and tends to skew toward open-weight models, so if Anthropic is dominating there, it's likely doing even better everywhere else.
